```{=tex}


\begin{abstract}
Conventional $\bar{X}$-$S$ charts and nonparametric median-MAD (median absolute deviation) charts can classify best-quality nondetectable (ND) cleaning validation (CV) events as out-of-control (OOC). A fundamental limitation is that conventional SPC assumes a one-cluster population where all observations share a common location-scale structure. In contrast, CV data may arise from a multicluster population because the same equipment is used to manufacture multiple products containing different active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) and therefore having different upper specification limits (USLs). ND observations are common and some clusters contain too few cleaning events to support reliable cluster-specific stability analysis.

This study develops a multicluster SPC theory for process stability analysis. The theory recognizes that observations may arise from multiple natural clusters and generalizes conventional SPC as the special case of one-cluster SPC. As a motivating application, CV data are considered, where cleaning events belong to natural API-defined clusters that may be ordered according to location or scale risk. A risk-based cluster-consolidation methodology is proposed for control-limit estimation, and the distribution-free d-cluster-calibrated stratified smoothed bootstrap univariate location (d-CCSSBU-L) and scale (d-CCSSBU-S) control charts are developed. Across real-world CV datasets, the d-CCSSBU charts avoided contradictory OOC classifications of ND events. Neither the d-CCSSBU charts nor the $\bar{X}$-$S$ charts uniformly exhibited ARL$_1$ superiority. The framework also supports evolutionary process monitoring, where the original process and its evolved version form distinct natural clusters, allowing continuous monitoring without restarting SPC following process changes. Collectively, the proposed theory and methods establish a multicluster SPC framework for stability assessment and ongoing monitoring.
\end{abstract}
```
\keywords{multicluster SPC, cleaning validation, USL-normalization, distribution-free, stratified smoothed bootstrap}

# Introduction

## Regulatory Expectations and SPC

Regulatory authorities and industry standards require pharmaceutical manufacturing processes and cleaning processes to be validated and maintained in a state of control [@FDA2014; @FDA2022multiuse; @CA2021; @APIC2021; @EMA2018; @ASTM_E3106; @ASTM_E2281; @ASTM_E2587; @ISPE2020; @FDACFR211]. Process stability and process capability assessments are therefore fundamental components of cleaning validation (CV). Manufacturers must demonstrate that a cleaning process consistently achieves acceptable residue removal throughout its lifecycle. However, although regulatory expectations require ongoing process monitoring and continued verification, regulatory documents generally do not prescribe a specific statistical methodology for assessing cleaning-process stability.

Statistical process control (SPC) is a well-established discipline in quality engineering and has been extensively discussed in standard textbooks and reference works [@Montgomery2020; @Qiu2014spc; @Chakraborti2019]. SPC methods have been required and applied in the pharmaceutical industry for process monitoring, trend analysis, and continued process verification [@FDA2014; @FDA2022multiuse; @CA2021; @APIC2021; @EMA2018; @ASTM_E3106; @ASTM_E2281; @ASTM_E2587; @ISPE2020; @Gershon1991; @Heigl2021].

## CV Data Characteristics

CV data have several characteristics that complicate conventional stability analysis. First, residue acceptance limits are product-specific and are commonly derived from different health-based exposure limits(HBEL) or permitted daily exposure (PDE) values [@EMA2018; @ASTME3219]. Observations generated by the same cleaning process may therefore be associated with different active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) and different upper specification limits (USLs) and may therefore not be directly comparable on their original measurement scales. Second, quantitative CV data accumulate through routine manufacturing rather than through a statistically designed experiment. Manufacturing frequency is driven by production schedules and market demand, while quantitative analytical testing is generally performed during qualification, verification or monitoring activities, investigations, process improvements, or selected product changeovers. Some API-specific datasets may therefore contain too few cleaning events to support reliable control-limit estimation or meaningful stability analysis. Third, CV data frequently contain substantial proportions of nondetectable (ND) observations. Following common industry practice, ND observations are often replaced by the corresponding limit of detection (LOD) or, when the LOD is unavailable, by the limit of quantification (LOQ). The resulting data may be highly right-skewed and exhibit a mixed discrete-continuous structure, with positive probability mass at substituted values. These characteristics complicate the application of parametric methods and may also limit rank-based nonparametric methods.

## Motivation for Multicluster SPC

Conventional SPC may be interpreted as a one-cluster framework, in which the monitored population is assumed to consist of a single relatively homogeneous event-generating cluster sharing a common location-scale structure and specification regime. Under this assumption, one location chart and one scale chart are sufficient to characterize both cluster stability and population stability. This framework is generally appropriate when SPC is applied to a single product, process, or quality attribute governed by one cluster.

Cleaning validation presents a different setting. A single validated cleaning process is routinely applied to multi-use equipment used to manufacture multiple products. For a given drug-active-ingredient residue category (DAR), all cleaning events collectively form a legitimate process population. However, because the equipment is used to manufacture multiple products, that population naturally contains product- or API-specific clusters. Consequently, a CV DAR population may be naturally multiclustered.


The practical consequences of ignoring this cluster structure are evident in the CV application. Conventional $\bar{X}$-$S$ charts generated numerous out-of-control (OOC, OC) signals for Equipment A and Equipment B, including signals for cleaning events consisting entirely of ND observations, as shown in the accompanying repository [@Yang2026dccssbu]. The same contradiction occurred with bootstrap-based median-MAD charts, where MAD denotes the median absolute deviation [@Yang2026dccssbu]. Because ND events represent best-quality cleaning outcomes, their classification as OOC cannot reasonably be interpreted as evidence of process deterioration. The occurrence of ND-event OOC signals under both conventional parametric and robust nonparametric charts suggests that the problem is not specific to a particular statistic or distributional assumption. Rather, it suggests a mismatch between the one-cluster reference structure of conventional SPC and the natural multicluster structure of CV population. The need for appropriate SPC methods for CV has also been recognized within the ASTM cleaning standards initiative, where an SPC standard for cleaning verification data has been identified as planned future work [@ASTM_Cleaning_Standards_2025].

These observations motivate multicluster SPC. In a multicluster population, characterization of a pooled population location and scale does not necessarily characterize the constituent clusters that generate the observed events. Process stability should therefore be established through the location and scale stability of the relevant clusters. Classical SPC is retained as the special case corresponding to a one-cluster population, whereas multicluster SPC extends the stability framework to populations containing multiple event-generating clusters.

When every cluster contains sufficient data, the direct solution is to construct separate location and scale charts for each cluster. When cluster-specific data are insufficient, scientifically similar clusters may instead be consolidated. However, determining how natural clusters should be consolidated without losing important process information remains a general research problem. CV data provide additional scientific structure that permits an application-specific solution. Because natural clusters are known through API identity and can be ordered according to location or scale risk, CV data permit a knowledge-driven, risk-based cluster consolidation strategy rather than an unsupervised cluster-discovery procedure.

More broadly, the multicluster SPC framework may also support lifecycle monitoring when planned process modifications, material substitutions, supplier changes, or other operational changes create multiple scientifically distinct but related event-generating conditions over time.

## Study Objectives and Contributions

Building on the specification-normalization framework developed for process capability analysis [@Yang2026sln], this study extends the framework to multicluster process stability analysis. USL-normalization expresses each residue measurement as a percentage of its corresponding USL, providing a common specification scale while preserving the natural cluster membership of individual cleaning events. This study makes the following contributions:

- It introduces multicluster SPC theory, under which classical SPC is recognized as the special case of one-cluster SPC.

- It establishes the natural cluster as the fundamental unit for characterizing location and scale stability in a multicluster population (Method 1 in Methods part).

- It develops a knowledge-driven, risk-based cluster-consolidation strategy for CV data in which API-specific clusters are ordered separately according to location and scale risk characteristics (Method 2 in Method part).

- It proposes distribution-free d-cluster-calibrated stratified smoothed bootstrap univariate location and scale charts, denoted by d-CCSSBU-L and d-CCSSBU-S. 

- It incorporates Poisson $u$ charts for microbial bioburden monitoring when the Poisson assumptions are supported; otherwise, the d-CCSSBU framework remains applicable.

Together with the developed capability-analysis framework [@Yang2026sln], the proposed methods provide a distribution-free multicluster framework for stability assessment, capability analysis, and ongoing monitoring of cleaning-validation processes. The framework is applicable both to naturally multiclustered CV populations and to manufacturing process lifecycle monitoring settings in which processes evolve over time.

# Methods

## Data and Code

The CV datasets for Equipment A and Equipment B are available in the accompanying GitHub repository [@Yang2026dccssbu]. The methods presented in this study were implemented in R, and the corresponding source code is available in the same repository [@Yang2026dccssbu].

## Multicluster SPC Theory {#sec-multicluster-spc}

### Realizable Events Arise from Natural Clusters {#sec-natural-clusters}

The term *cluster* has different meanings in different disciplines. In survey sampling, a cluster is a grouping of population units that serves as a sampling unit within a sampling design [@Lohr2021sampling]. For example, churches, schools, households, or geographic areas may be treated as clusters, with sampling performed at the cluster level before sampling individual units within selected clusters. Although not part of the definition itself, efficient cluster-sampling designs often prefer clusters whose members are heterogeneous so that each cluster reasonably reflects the diversity of the target population [@Lohr2021sampling]. In contrast, cluster analysis and unsupervised learning use the term to denote a group of observations that are relatively similar to one another and distinct from observations in other groups [@Kaufman1990; @Kabacoff2022].

The present work is closer to the latter interpretation but differs in an important respect. The clusters considered here are not statistical groupings discovered from observed data. Rather, they are natural clusters whose memberships are known *a priori* from scientific or operational knowledge. Each natural cluster represents a distinct event-generating structure within the population, and different clusters may arise from different underlying generating mechanisms. The objective is therefore not cluster discovery but determination of whether known natural clusters can be monitored separately or consolidated into a shared control-chart reference structure.


A natural cluster here is a scientifically or operationally meaningful subgroup within a population whose events are generated under a common event-generating mechanism. Events within the same natural cluster share the underlying conditions that produce the observed outcomes, whereas events from different natural clusters arise from distinct event-generating mechanisms. Every realizable event is generated from a single natural cluster, and the observed characteristics of that event reflect the structure of the generating cluster. Natural clusters are properties of the underlying event-generating system rather than statistical partitions created by an analyst. A population may contain one or more naturally existing clusters. Let $\mathcal{P}=\{\mathcal{C}_1,\mathcal{C}_2,\ldots,\mathcal{C}_q\}$, where $\mathcal{C}_i$ denotes the $i$th  constituent natural cluster and $q$ denotes the number of clusters. Every realizable event is therefore generated within a constituent cluster rather than by arbitrarily combining characteristics selected independently from the entire population. This distinction is not apparent when $q=1$ but it becomes essential when $q>1$, because a realizable event must preserve the internal structure of the cluster from which it arises. 

**Example 1: Gene populations and biological species.** Consider a global gene population, denoted by $\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{gene}}=\{\mathcal{C}_1,\mathcal{C}_2,\ldots,\mathcal{C}_q\}$, where each cluster $\mathcal{C}_i$ represents the genetic system associated with a particular biological species. The overall gene population exists, but it is naturally organized into species-specific clusters. A realizable organism is generated from the coordinated genetic structure of a single species. For example, a human organism is generated from the human genetic system, not from a collection of genes independently sampled from humans, dogs, cats, and other species. Although all sampled genes originate from the overall gene population, their arbitrary combination would not necessarily correspond to any species $\mathcal{C}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{C}_q$ and may not represent a viable organism. The key issue is therefore not the existence of the overall gene population. Rather, valid organisms preserve the integrated genetic structure of a particular species-level cluster. Membership in the overall population does not make genes freely interchangeable across species. Species therefore represent naturally existing event-generating clusters rather than groups created retrospectively for analytical convenience.

**Example 2: Cleaning-validation DAR population.** Consider one cleaning process performed on a particular equipment unit. All DAR results obtained from this cleaning process collectively form one process population, denoted by $\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{DAR}}$. Suppose that the equipment is used to manufacture $q$ different API products. The DAR population can then be represented by $\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{DAR}}=\{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR},1},\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR},2},\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR},q}\}$, where $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR},i}$ contains the DAR events associated with the $i$th API residue. Thus, the DAR population from a single cleaning process naturally contains $q$ API-specific DAR clusters. Each DAR event arises under the integrated cleaning and analytical conditions associated with a particular API. These conditions may include API identity, residue behavior, reporting limit, censoring pattern, specification basis, and other factors that jointly define the context under which a DAR event is generated and interpreted. If event characteristics are sampled separately from different API-specific DAR clusters and combined into a synthetic event, the resulting combination may not belong to any of $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR},1},\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR},q}$. Although every characteristic originates from the overall DAR population, the constructed event may not be realizable under any actual API-specific cleaning condition. The cluster structure follows from the scientific and operational mechanism that generates CV events; it is not imposed retrospectively for statistical convenience.

### Classical SPC as One-Cluster SPC {#sec-one-cluster-spc}

Process stability has two complementary characteristics: location and scale. Location stability concerns whether the process center remains statistically predictable over time, whereas scale stability concerns whether process dispersion remains statistically predictable. 

Classical SPC can be interpreted as one-cluster SPC with the monitored population defined as $\mathcal{P}=\{\mathcal{C}_1\}$. Therefore, characterization of $\mathcal{C}_1$ is equivalent to characterization of $\mathcal{P}$. Consequently, a single location statistic and a single scale statistic are sufficient to monitor population stability.

This equivalence no longer holds when the population is naturally multiclustered. Let $\mathcal{P}=\{\mathcal{C}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{C}_q\}$ with $q>1$. Although population-level location and scale summaries may still be calculated, they do not necessarily represent the location and scale characteristics of the constituent clusters that generate the observed events. Because events arise within clusters, process stability must be established through cluster-level location and scale stability rather than solely through population-level summaries. If all relevant clusters are controlled with respect to both location and scale, then the population composed of those clusters is controlled. This principle may be summarized as $\text{cluster-level location and scale control} \Longrightarrow \text{population-level process control}$.

The practical consequences of ignoring natural cluster structure are illustrated by the CV application. Conventional population-level $\bar{X}$-$S$ and bootstrap median-MAD charts produced OOC signals for best-quality ND cleaning events [@Yang2026dccssbu]. Because ND events represent the lowest-risk cleaning outcomes, such signals are difficult to reconcile with known process characteristics. This observation supports the theoretical proposition that, for naturally multiclustered populations, the cluster rather than the aggregated population is the fundamental unit of process characterization and stability monitoring.

### General Multicluster SPC Methods {#sec-general-multicluster-methods}

For a multicluster population represented by $\mathcal{P}=\{\mathcal{C}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{C}_q\}$, the monitoring method must preserve the natural cluster structure. Two general methods may be considered, depending on the amount of information available within each cluster. Method 1 is preferred because it fully preserves the natural cluster structure, whereas Method 2 is primarily motivated by data-sparsity considerations.

**Method 1: One Cluster, One Control Chart.** When every natural cluster contains sufficient data, the most direct implementation is to monitor each cluster separately. Cluster $\mathcal{C}_i$ is treated as a cluster-level population with its own location and scale charts. Stability of the overall population is established through the stability of all constituent clusters. This method fully preserves the original cluster structure and provides direct cluster-specific characterization of process location and scale. It represents the ideal implementation of multicluster SPC when data-size restrictions are absent. The method may be implemented as multiple separate charts or as a unified chart containing multiple cluster-specific reference structures. Under the unified implementation, cluster $\mathcal{C}_i$ has its own $\mathrm{LCL}_i$, $\mathrm{CL}_i$, and $\mathrm{UCL}_i$, and an event from that cluster is evaluated only against its corresponding limits. The separate-chart and unified-chart implementations are theoretically equivalent because both assess stability at the natural-cluster level.

**Method 2: Consolidation of Natural Clusters.** When some natural clusters contain insufficient observations, scientifically or statistically similar clusters may be consolidated before chart construction. Let the original population be represented by $\mathcal{P}=\{\mathcal{C}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{C}_q\}$. A consolidation procedure may produce $m$ merged clusters, denoted by $\mathcal{G}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{G}_m$, where $m<q$ and each $\mathcal{G}_j$ contains one or more natural clusters. If the resulting merged clusters contain sufficient data, one location chart and one scale chart can be constructed for each $\mathcal{G}_j$. Cluster consolidation is supported by the cluster-analysis literature [@Kaufman1990; @Kabacoff2022]. Common methods include hierarchical clustering [@Johnson1967], k-means clustering [@MacQueen1967], density-based clustering [@Ester1996], and model-based clustering [@Fraley2002]. These conventional methods are generally unsupervised learning methods designed to discover cluster structures when membership is unknown. In multicluster SPC, however, the natural clusters may already be defined through scientific or operational knowledge. The objective is therefore not to discover clusters but to determine whether known clusters can be appropriately consolidated to share a control-chart reference structure.

Cluster consolidation is consistent with the operation of a control chart. A control chart does not require every event to have an identical observed location or scale; rather, it permits expected variation within the in-control region. Therefore, natural clusters with sufficiently similar location or scale behavior may share a reference structure, provided that consolidation does not generate scientifically inappropriate OOC classifications or an unacceptable loss of detection performance.

**Remaining Research Challenges.** Method 2 does not provide a universal solution. First, the merged clusters may still contain insufficient observations for reliable control-limit estimation. Second, further consolidation may combine clusters with meaningfully different location or scale characteristics and cause routine events from one or more natural clusters to be classified as OOC. Third, different clustering or consolidation methods may produce different merged structures, monitoring systems, and stability conclusions. Finally, clusters considered sufficiently similar for location monitoring may not be sufficiently similar for scale monitoring, implying that different consolidation structures may be required for location and scale control charts. Therefore, a general rule for determining which natural clusters should be consolidated, how many merged clusters should be retained, and when consolidation has become excessive remains an open research area in multicluster SPC.

**Application 1 of Method 2: Evolutionary Process Monitoring.** Method 2 supports continuous evolutionary process monitoring. Process improvements, equipment modifications, material substitutions, supplier changes, analytical-method updates, automation upgrades, and other planned operational changes may create an evolved process that is treated as a new process from a GMP perspective. This situation commonly arises in lifecycle monitoring, where the evolved process contains insufficient observations to support standalone SPC implementation. The ability to assess process stability as early as possible during process evolution can provide substantial operational and quality benefits. Although the evolved process reflects a modified event-generating mechanism, it often remains similar to its predecessor. Under the multicluster framework, the original process is treated as one natural cluster and the evolved process as another. When predefined consolidation criteria are satisfied, the clusters may share a common monitoring structure while preserving their identities as distinct clusters.

The CAR data for Equipment B illustrate this application. A cleaning-agent replacement occurred after Event 80, creating a new event-generating condition for Events 81 to 91 (Figure \ref{fig:d-ccssbu-car-equipment-ab}). From a GMP perspective, this change created a new process state and therefore a distinct natural cluster. Nevertheless, the d-CCSSBU analysis demonstrated that the evolved process remained sufficiently consistent with the original process to permit cluster consolidation. No inappropriate OOC signals were observed, and the control chart provided no obvious indication that a process change had occurred. This result suggests that the replacement cleaning agent achieved performance comparable to that of the original agent, thereby supporting continuous SPC monitoring without restarting the monitoring program from scratch.

By permitting appropriate consolidation of related natural clusters, the method reduces statistical monitoring gaps associated with data reaccumulation following process changes while preserving the identity of each process state. This application complements, but does not replace, the formal change-control, qualification, validation, and continued-process-verification activities required under the applicable pharmaceutical quality system.


**Application 2 of Method 2: Naturally Multiclustered Cleaning Validation.** The primary application examined in this study is monitoring naturally multiclustered CV processes. In CV, natural clusters are typically defined through API identity and therefore possess a clear scientific interpretation. Moreover, the clusters can be ordered according to cleaning risk, providing a unique opportunity to develop a risk-based realization of Method 2 in which higher-risk clusters are used for chart calibration and lower-risk clusters are evaluated against the resulting reference structure. The d-CCSSBU-L and d-CCSSBU-S charts developed in this study operationalize this concept and provide a practical framework for SPC implementation in multicluster CV environments. The CV-specific realization is described in the following sections.

### CV-Specific Multicluster SPC Realization {#sec-cv-multicluster-spc}

CV provides a setting in which natural clusters are defined through API identity and possess a natural risk ordering. For location monitoring, clusters are ordered using their cluster-level location statistics. A cluster with a larger location represents higher residual levels and therefore greater cleaning risk. For scale monitoring, clusters are ordered using their cluster-level scale statistics. A cluster with greater dispersion represents greater process uncertainty and therefore greater risk. Let the ordered clusters be represented by $\mathcal{C}_{(1)},\mathcal{C}_{(2)},\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{(q)}$, where $\mathcal{C}_{(1)}$ denotes the highest-risk cluster and subsequent clusters represent progressively lower-risk conditions.

As a CV-specific realization of the general multicluster SPC framework, define the calibration set as $\mathcal{D}_d=\{\mathcal{C}_{(1)},\mathcal{C}_{(2)},\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{(d)}\}$, where $d$ denotes the number of highest-risk ordered clusters retained for chart calibration. The set $\mathcal{D}_d$ is used to estimate the chart center line and control limits, and $d$ is termed the heterogeneity index. Larger values of $d$ incorporate greater cluster heterogeneity into calibration, whereas smaller values focus calibration on the highest-risk clusters. An admissible heterogeneity index $d$ must satisfy the following three principles.

**Rule 1: ND-Event Protection.** ND events represent acceptable and generally best-quality cleaning outcomes. Therefore, an ND event should not be classified as OOC. Any candidate value of $d$ that produces ND-event OOC signals is inadmissible. This rule ensures consistency between the scientific interpretation of ND results and the statistical interpretation produced by the control chart.

**Rule 2: Stage 3A Event Protection.** Stage 3A events are used to establish baseline process characteristics and should remain within the calibrated control structure whenever feasible. Candidate values of $d$ that avoid Stage 3A OOC classifications are preferred. Complete protection may not always be attainable. When all candidate values of $d$ produce one or more Stage 3A OOC signals, the signals cannot be attributed solely to the choice of $d$ and should be reported transparently. In such cases, the persistent Stage 3A OOC events may indicate genuine departures from the assumed baseline process condition and should be investigated rather than eliminated through further calibration adjustments. Candidate selection should then proceed according to the remaining protection and detection-performance criteria.

**Rule 3: Benchmark-Referenced OOC Detection Performance and Heterogeneity Retention.** Protection of ND and Stage 3A events must not substantially reduce sensitivity to meaningful process changes. Therefore, admissible values of $d$ are evaluated relative to the corresponding conventional SPC benchmark. For location monitoring, the benchmark is the conventional $\bar X$ chart. For scale monitoring, the benchmark is the conventional $S$ chart. Candidate values of $d$ are evaluated over a prespecified range of practically relevant shift magnitudes. When multiple admissible values of $d$ exhibit ARL$_1$ performance that is no worse than the corresponding benchmark across the complete shift range, preference is given to the largest value of $d$ because it incorporates greater cluster heterogeneity into calibration while maintaining satisfactory detection performance. Conversely, when no admissible value of $d$ exhibits benchmark-level performance across the complete shift range, preference is given to the admissible candidate with the most favorable relative ARL$_1$ performance. If multiple candidates provide equivalent relative ARL$_1$ performance, preference is again given to the largest value of $d$ because it incorporates greater cluster heterogeneity without sacrificing detection performance. This principle selects the recommended heterogeneity index $d$ by jointly considering benchmark-referenced OOC detection performance and retention of cluster heterogeneity within the calibration structure.

The proposed framework adopts the Shewhart Rule 1 signaling criterion, whereby an event is classified as potentially out-of-control when it exceeds the upper control limit. Additional WECO-type runs rules are not used. CV data are naturally bounded below by zero, and smaller residue values correspond to improved cleaning performance rather than undesirable process conditions. Consequently, the primary concern is detection of increases in residue levels or variability rather than departures in both directions. Many conventional runs rules were developed for two-sided process monitoring and therefore have limited interpretation in the present setting. The framework therefore uses UCL exceedance as the primary operational definition of a potential OOC signal (see Section 2.2 of [@Chakraborti2009precedence]).

This calibration strategy reflects the risk hierarchy inherent in CV by estimating control limits from the highest-risk ordered clusters. As a result, a single chart can be used to monitor the population without requiring separate charts for every cluster. The CV-specific multicluster SPC realization described above establishes the conceptual framework for risk-based cluster calibration. The corresponding operational implementation is provided by the d-cluster-calibrated stratified smoothed bootstrap univariate location (d-CCSSBU-L) and scale (d-CCSSBU-S) charts. The following methodology section translates this framework into explicit chart-construction algorithms, calibration procedures, benchmark comparisons, and heterogeneity-index selection methods.

## d-CCSSBU Methodology

### Prospective or Retrospective Monitoring {#sec-monitoring-stages}

\textcolor{blue}{Process monitoring may be conducted prospectively or retrospectively. All events are time ordered. In prospective monitoring, the analysis proceeds sequentially from Stage 3A to Stage 3B. Stage 3A analysis, corresponding to Phase I SPC} [@Qiu2014spc], \textcolor{blue}{establishes the initial reference, whereas Stage 3B analysis, corresponding to Phase II SPC} [@Qiu2014spc], \textcolor{blue}{applies this reference to monitor or verify newly generated events in real time or at predefined intervals. However, multicluster SPC may have an intermediate stage where both Stage 3A and Stage 3B exist for different clusters. Most references recommend 20--30 events} [@Montgomery2020; @Qiu2014spc; @Chakraborti2019] \textcolor{blue}{for Stage 3A (Phase I); however, we temporarily set $n_{3A}=10$ (see explanation in Discussion section). Retrospective analysis utilizes all available historical and current events to evaluate process stability and capability over the period up to the analysis time point.}

\textcolor{blue}{The proposed control-chart framework below and the capability-analysis framework developed in} [@Yang2026sln] \textcolor{blue}{can therefore be applied to either prospective Stage 3A/Stage 3B monitoring or retrospective analysis, with the latter implemented by setting $n_{3A}$ equal to the total number of available events and $n_{3B}=0$ in the following algorithm.}


### Common Steps for d-CCSSBU Chart Construction Algorithms {#sec-common-steps}

Let $D=\{e_1,e_2,\ldots,e_x\}$ denote the chronological sequence of cleaning events, where $e_t$ denotes the event observed at event-time index $t$. The following algorithm establishes the common framework for d-CCSSBU-L and d-CCSSBU-S chart construction for a fixed ordered-cluster parameter $d$. Selection of the optimal process-specific value of $d$ is addressed separately in the performance-optimization procedure.

**Step 1. Replace non-detects.** \textcolor{blue}{If any ND observations are present, replace them with the corresponding LOD or, when unavailable, the LOQ. (This conservative, worst-case replacement is commonly used in practice and is consistent with the general regulatory principle of applying scientifically justified, conservative treatment when exact quantitative information is unavailable. However, Step 1 does not depend on this particular substitution; other scientifically justified approaches for handling ND observations can also be used.)}

**Step 2. Conduct USL normalization.** Normalize each residue observation using $Z_{ti}=100X_{ti}/\mathrm{USL}_{ti}$. The resulting values are expressed as percentages of the applicable USL.

**Step 3. Calculate event-level location and scale statistics.** For the USL-normalized observations $R_t=\{Z_{t1},Z_{t2},\ldots,Z_{tp}\}$ associated with event $e_t$, calculate the location statistic of $e_t$ as $L_t=\mathrm{median}(R_t)$ and the scale statistic of $e_t$ as $S_t=\mathrm{MAD}(R_t)=\mathrm{median}\{|Z_{ti}-\mathrm{median}(R_t)|:i=1,\ldots,p\}$. 

**Step 4. Create nominal Stage 3A and Stage 3B datasets.** Let $n_{3A}$ denote the target number of Stage 3A calibration events. If $x=n_{3A}$, define $D_{\mathrm{3A}}=\{e_1,\ldots,e_x\}$ and $D_{\mathrm{3B}}=\emptyset$. If $x>n_{3A}$, define $D_{\mathrm{3A}}=\{e_1,\ldots,e_{n_{3A}}\}$ and $D_{\mathrm{3B}}=\{e_{n_{3A}+1},\ldots,e_x\}$.

**Step 5. Create DAR clusters.** \textcolor{blue}{Retain a cleaning event for calibration if $\max_{i=1,\ldots,p}Z_{ti}\le100$, where 100 corresponds to 100\% of the applicable USL. Thus, all observations within the applicable specification remain eligible for calibration consideration, whereas an event containing an OOS observation is excluded from baseline calibration. For residue type DAR$_j$, create the DAR cluster $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_j}=\{e_t:e_t\in D,\ \max_{i=1,\ldots,p}Z_{ti} \le 100,\ \text{and is associated with DAR}_j\}$. Let $q$ denote the total number of DAR clusters represented in the calibration-eligible dataset. The DAR clusters form a partition of the calibration-eligible events, such that each calibration-eligible event belongs to exactly one DAR cluster. The parameter $d$, where $1\le d\le q$, denotes the number of ordered DAR clusters incorporated into chart calibration.}

### d-CCSSBU-L Chart Construction Algorithm {#sec-dccssbu-l-algorithm}

The d-CCSSBU-L chart is constructed through above Steps 1--5 and Steps 6--15 below.

**Step 6. Order DAR clusters by location.** For each DAR cluster, compute the cluster-level location statistic as $L_{\mathrm{DAR}_j}=\mathrm{median}\{L_t:e_t\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_j}\}$. Order the DAR clusters such that $L_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(1)}}\ge L_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(2)}}\ge\cdots\ge L_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(q)}}$, where $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(1)}},\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(2)}},\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(q)}}$ denote the resulting ordered DAR clusters.

**Step 7. Identify Stage 3A events within ordered DAR clusters.** For each ordered cluster $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(j)}}$, identify its nominal Stage 3A component as $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(j)},3A}=\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(j)}}\cap D_{\mathrm{3A}}$. Cluster $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(j)}}$ may have an empty Stage 3A component if no event in it occurs during the nominal Stage 3A period.

**Step 8. Build the d-CCSSBU-L calibration dataset.** For a selected value $d\in\{1,2,\ldots,q\}$, construct the calibration dataset as $D_{\mathrm{Cal,L}}(d)=\bigcup_{j=1}^{d}D_{\mathrm{Cal,L},j}(d)$, where each $D_{\mathrm{Cal,L},j}(d)$ is constructed from ordered DAR cluster $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(j)}}$ using Steps 8.1--8.3.

**Step 8.1. Order events within each selected cluster.** Order events in $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(j)}}$ by decreasing event-level location statistic $L_t$.

**Step 8.2. Select events with distinct $L_t$ values.** Select events with distinct $L_t$ values from largest to smallest until either $|D_{\mathrm{Cal,L},j}(d)|=n_{3A}$ or no additional distinct $L_t$ values remain. If multiple events share the same $L_t$ value, prioritize events belonging to $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(j)},3A}$. If multiple Stage 3A events remain tied, select the earliest chronological event.

**Step 8.3. Fill remaining positions using remaining events.** If fewer than $n_{3A}$ events have been selected after Step 8.2, repeat Step 8.2 on the remaining unselected events in $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(j)}}$ until either $|D_{\mathrm{Cal,L},j}(d)|=n_{3A}$ or all available events have been exhausted.

Consequently, each selected ordered DAR cluster contributes up to $n_{3A}$ calibration events and $|D_{\mathrm{Cal,L},j}(d)|=\min(n_{3A},n_j)$, where $n_j=|\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(j)}}|$.

**Step 9. Classify calibration status.** Let $n_{\mathrm{Cal},j}=|D_{\mathrm{Cal,L},j}(d)|$ denote the achieved calibration size for selected cluster $j$ and $D_{\mathrm{Aug,L}}(d)=D_{\mathrm{Cal,L}}(d)\setminus D_{\mathrm{3A}}$ be the augmentation set. A selected ordered DAR cluster is classified as calibration-complete if $n_{\mathrm{Cal},j}=n_{3A}$ and calibration-limited if $n_{\mathrm{Cal},j}<n_{3A}$ after all currently available events have been exhausted. The calibration status is classified into one of the following five cases.

**Case 1: Initial Stage 3A complete.** If $x=n_{3A}$ and every selected ordered DAR cluster is calibration-complete, then the calibration dataset is finalized using the available events.

**Case 2: Initial Stage 3A calibration limited.** If $x=n_{3A}$ and at least one selected ordered DAR cluster is calibration-limited, then the calibration dataset remains provisional because no post-Stage 3A events are available.

**Case 3: Stage 3B available and finalized without supplementation.** If $x>n_{3A}$, every selected ordered DAR cluster is calibration-complete, and $D_{\mathrm{Aug,L}}(d)=\emptyset$, then the calibration dataset is finalized without using post-Stage 3A events.

**Case 4: Stage 3B available and finalized with supplementation.** If $x>n_{3A}$, every selected ordered DAR cluster is calibration-complete, and $D_{\mathrm{Aug,L}}(d)\neq\emptyset$, then the calibration dataset is finalized after incorporating selected post-Stage 3A events contained in $D_{\mathrm{Aug,L}}(d)$.

**Case 5: Stage 3B available and calibration still provisional.** If $x>n_{3A}$ and at least one selected ordered DAR cluster remains calibration-limited after all currently available events have been exhausted, then the calibration dataset remains provisional and may be updated when additional eligible events become available.

**Step 10. Create sampling-location calibration strata.** Let $n_{\mathrm{Cal}}=|D_{\mathrm{Cal,L}}(d)|$ denote the size of the calibration dataset. For sampling location $r_s=1,\ldots,p$, create the calibration stratum $G_{r_s}=\{Z_{ir_s}:e_i\in D_{\mathrm{Cal,L}}(d)\}$. The calibration dataset is therefore partitioned into sampling-location strata $G_1,G_2,\ldots,G_p$.

**Step 11. Generate CCSSB bootstrap events.** For bootstrap replicate $b=1,\ldots,B$, sample one observation with replacement from each calibration stratum $G_{r_s}$ to obtain $X_{br_s}\in G_{r_s}$ for $r_s=1,\ldots,p$. Form the bootstrap event $e_b=\{X_{b1},X_{b2},\ldots,X_{bp}\}$ and smooth each sampled observation using $X_{br_s}^{*}=\max\{0,X_{br_s}+\varepsilon_{br_s}\}$, where $\varepsilon_{br_s}\sim N(0,h_{r_s}^{2})$ and $h_{r_s}=\max\{c_{\mathrm{smooth}}\times\mathrm{MAD}(G_{r_s}),h_{\min}\}$. In this study, $c_{\mathrm{smooth}}=0.5$, $h_{\min}=0.05$, and $B=20{,}000$. The resulting smoothed bootstrap event is $e_b^{*}=\{X_{b1}^{*},X_{b2}^{*},\ldots,X_{bp}^{*}\}$. The smoothing constant $c_{\mathrm{smooth}}=0.5$ and minimum bandwidth $h_{\min}=0.05$ were selected from a grid of candidate values based on the stability of bootstrap control-limit estimates and the consistency of charting conclusions across the study datasets. The bootstrap size $B=20{,}000$ was chosen to provide stable estimation of the upper-tail quantiles required for control-limit calibration. These quantities are implementation parameters rather than fixed methodological constants, and users may specify alternative values in the software implementation.

**Step 12. Calculate bootstrap location statistics.** For each bootstrap replicate $b=1,\ldots,B$, calculate the bootstrap event-level location statistic as $L_b^{*}=\mathrm{median}(X_{b1}^{*},X_{b2}^{*},\ldots,X_{bp}^{*})$. The collection $\{L_1^{*},L_2^{*},\ldots,L_B^{*}\}$ represents the CCSSB-calibrated location distribution associated with $D_{\mathrm{Cal,L}}(d)$.

**Step 13. Estimate d-CCSSBU-L chart parameters.** Using the bootstrap location statistics, estimate the center line as $CL_{\mathrm{CCSSBU-L-boot}}=\mathrm{median}(L_1^{*},L_2^{*},\ldots,L_B^{*})$ and estimate the upper control limit as $UCL_{\mathrm{CCSSBU-L-boot}}=\hat q_{1-\alpha}(L_1^{*},L_2^{*},\ldots,L_B^{*})$, where $\alpha=1/\mathrm{ARL}_0$ and $\hat q_{1-\alpha}$ denotes the empirical $(1-\alpha)$ quantile. In this study, $\mathrm{ARL}_0=740$ and therefore $\alpha=1/740$.

**Step 14. Construct the d-CCSSBU-L chart.** Calculate the event-level location statistic $L_t$ for each cleaning event and plot the chronological sequence $\{L_1,L_2,\ldots,L_x\}$ together with $CL_{\mathrm{CCSSBU-L-boot}}$ and $UCL_{\mathrm{CCSSBU-L-boot}}$. Classify event $e_t$ as potentially out-of-control whenever $L_t>UCL_{\mathrm{CCSSBU-L-boot}}$.

**Step 15. Perform Stage 3B monitoring.** Under Case 3 or Case 4, finalize the calibration dataset and chart parameters and apply them unchanged throughout routine Stage 3B monitoring. Under Case 3, all events in $D_{\mathrm{3B}}$ are monitored. Under Case 4, events contained in $D_{\mathrm{Aug,L}}(d)$ are used only for calibration and are excluded from routine monitoring. Under Case 2 or Case 5, maintain provisional calibration status until sufficient eligible events become available to finalize the chart.

### d-CCSSBU-S Chart Construction Algorithm {#sec-dccssbu-s-algorithm}

The d-CCSSBU-S chart is constructed through above Steps 1--5 and Steps 6--15 below.

**Step 6. Order DAR clusters by scale.** For each DAR cluster, calculate the cluster-level scale statistic as $S_{\mathrm{DAR}_j}=\mathrm{median}\{S_t:e_t\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_j}\}$. Order the DAR clusters such that $S_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(1)}}\ge S_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(2)}}\ge\cdots\ge S_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(q)}}$, where $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(1)}},\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(2)}},\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(q)}}$ denote the resulting ordered DAR clusters.

**Step 7. Identify Stage 3A events within ordered DAR clusters.** For each ordered DAR cluster $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(j)}}$, identify its nominal Stage 3A component as $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(j)},3A}=\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(j)}}\cap D_{\mathrm{3A}}$. Cluster $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(j)}}$ may have an empty Stage 3A component if no event from it occurs during the nominal Stage 3A period.

**Step 8. Build the d-CCSSBU-S calibration dataset.** For $d\in\{1,2,\ldots,q\}$, construct the calibration dataset as $D_{\mathrm{Cal,S}}(d)=\bigcup_{j=1}^{d}D_{\mathrm{Cal,S},j}(d)$, where each $D_{\mathrm{Cal,S},j}(d)$ is constructed from ordered DAR cluster $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(j)}}$ using Steps 8.1--8.3.

**Step 8.1. Order events within each selected cluster.** Order all events in $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(j)}}$ by decreasing event-level scale statistic $S_t$.

**Step 8.2. Select events with distinct $S_t$ values.** Select events with distinct $S_t$ values from largest to smallest until either $|D_{\mathrm{Cal,S},j}(d)|=n_{3A}$ or no additional distinct $S_t$ values remain. If multiple events share the same $S_t$ value, prioritize events belonging to $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(j)},3A}$. If multiple Stage 3A events remain tied, select the earliest chronological event.

**Step 8.3. Fill remaining positions using remaining events.** If fewer than $n_{3A}$ events have been selected after Step 8.2, repeat Step 8.2 on the remaining unselected events in $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(j)}}$ until either $|D_{\mathrm{Cal,S},j}(d)|=n_{3A}$ or all available events have been exhausted.

Consequently, each selected ordered DAR cluster contributes up to $n_{3A}$ calibration events, such that $|D_{\mathrm{Cal,S},j}(d)|=\min(n_{3A},n_j)$, where $n_j=|\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(j)}}|$. 

**Step 9. Classify calibration status.** Let $n_{\mathrm{Cal},j}=|D_{\mathrm{Cal,S},j}(d)|$ denote the achieved calibration size for selected cluster $j$ and $D_{\mathrm{Aug,S}}(d)=D_{\mathrm{Cal,S}}(d)\setminus D_{\mathrm{3A}}$ be the augmentation set. An ordered DAR cluster $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{DAR}_{(j)}}$ is classified as calibration-complete if $n_{\mathrm{Cal},j}=n_{3A}$ and calibration-limited if $n_{\mathrm{Cal},j}<n_{3A}$ after all currently available events have been exhausted. The calibration status is classified into one of the following five cases.

**Case 1: Initial Stage 3A complete.** If $x=n_{3A}$ and every selected ordered DAR cluster is calibration-complete, then the calibration dataset is finalized using the available events.

**Case 2: Initial Stage 3A calibration limited.** If $x=n_{3A}$ and at least one selected ordered DAR cluster is calibration-limited, then the calibration dataset remains provisional because no post-Stage 3A events are available.

**Case 3: Stage 3B available and finalized without supplementation.** If $x>n_{3A}$, every selected ordered DAR cluster is calibration-complete, and $D_{\mathrm{Aug,S}}(d)=\emptyset$, then the calibration dataset is finalized without using post-Stage 3A events.

**Case 4: Stage 3B available and finalized with supplementation.** If $x>n_{3A}$, every selected ordered DAR cluster is calibration-complete, and $D_{\mathrm{Aug,S}}(d)\neq\emptyset$, then the calibration dataset is finalized after incorporating selected post-Stage 3A events contained in $D_{\mathrm{Aug,S}}(d)$.

**Case 5: Stage 3B available and calibration still provisional.** If $x>n_{3A}$ and at least one selected ordered DAR cluster remains calibration-limited after all currently available events have been exhausted, then the calibration dataset remains provisional and may be updated when additional eligible events become available.

**Step 10. Create sampling-location calibration strata.** Let $n_{\mathrm{Cal}}=|D_{\mathrm{Cal,S}}(d)|$ denote the size of the calibration dataset. For sampling location $r_s=1,\ldots,p$, create the calibration stratum $G_{r_s}=\{Z_{ir_s}:e_i\in D_{\mathrm{Cal,S}}(d)\}$. The calibration dataset is therefore partitioned into sampling-location strata $G_1,G_2,\ldots,G_p$.

**Step 11. Generate CCSSB bootstrap events.** For bootstrap replicate $b=1,\ldots,B$, sample one observation with replacement from each calibration stratum $G_{r_s}$ to obtain $X_{br_s}\in G_{r_s}$ for $r_s=1,\ldots,p$. Form the bootstrap event $e_b=\{X_{b1},X_{b2},\ldots,X_{bp}\}$ and smooth each sampled observation using $X_{br_s}^{*}=\max\{0,X_{br_s}+\varepsilon_{br_s}\}$, where $\varepsilon_{br_s}\sim N(0,h_{r_s}^{2})$ and $h_{r_s}=\max\{c_{\mathrm{smooth}}\times\mathrm{MAD}(G_{r_s}),h_{\min}\}$. In this study, $c_{\mathrm{smooth}}=0.5$, $h_{\min}=0.05$, and $B=20{,}000$. The resulting smoothed bootstrap event is $e_b^{*}=\{X_{b1}^{*},X_{b2}^{*},\ldots,X_{bp}^{*}\}$.

**Step 12. Calculate bootstrap scale statistics.** For each bootstrap replicate $b=1,\ldots,B$, calculate the bootstrap event-level scale statistic as $S_b^{*}=\mathrm{MAD}(X_{b1}^{*},X_{b2}^{*},\ldots,X_{bp}^{*})$. The collection $\{S_1^{*},S_2^{*},\ldots,S_B^{*}\}$ represents the CCSSB-calibrated scale distribution associated with $D_{\mathrm{Cal,S}}(d)$.

**Step 13. Estimate d-CCSSBU-S chart parameters.** Using the bootstrap scale statistics, estimate the center line as $CL_{\mathrm{CCSSBU-S-boot}}=\mathrm{median}(S_1^{*},S_2^{*},\ldots,S_B^{*})$ and estimate the upper control limit as $UCL_{\mathrm{CCSSBU-S-boot}}=\hat q_{1-\alpha}(S_1^{*},S_2^{*},\ldots,S_B^{*})$, where $\alpha=1/\mathrm{ARL}_0$ and $\hat q_{1-\alpha}$ denotes the empirical $(1-\alpha)$ quantile. In this study, $\mathrm{ARL}_0=740$ and therefore $\alpha=1/740$.

**Step 14. Construct the d-CCSSBU-S chart.** Calculate the event-level scale statistic $S_t$ for each cleaning event and plot the chronological sequence $\{S_1,S_2,\ldots,S_x\}$ together with $CL_{\mathrm{CCSSBU-S-boot}}$ and $UCL_{\mathrm{CCSSBU-S-boot}}$. Classify event $e_t$ as potentially out-of-control whenever $S_t>UCL_{\mathrm{CCSSBU-S-boot}}$.

**Step 15. Perform Stage 3B monitoring.** Under Case 3 or Case 4, finalize the calibration dataset and chart parameters and apply them unchanged throughout routine Stage 3B monitoring. Under Case 3, all events in $D_{\mathrm{3B}}$ are monitored. Under Case 4, events contained in $D_{\mathrm{Aug,S}}(d)$ are used only for calibration and are excluded from routine monitoring. Under Case 2 or Case 5, maintain provisional calibration status until sufficient eligible events become available to finalize the chart.

**Remark on d-CCSSBU-L and d-CCSSBU-S charts.** The proposed framework is presented using DAR data but may also be applied to CAR or Mic data when scientifically meaningful cluster heterogeneity exists. When the monitored population contains only one natural cluster such that $q=1$ and therefore $d=1$, the proposed methodology reduces to the corresponding one-cluster bootstrap location and scale charts.

### Selection of $d$ for the d-CCSSBU-L Chart {#sec-d-select-l}

For a given residue type, such as DAR, the following procedure evaluates candidate values of $d$ under additive location shifts and recommends a preferred value of $d$.

**Step 1. Construct d-CCSSBU-L charts for specific $d$.** Apply the d-CCSSBU-L chart construction algorithm in @sec-dccssbu-l-algorithm for each candidate value $d\in\{1,\ldots,q\}$. For each candidate $d$, obtain $D_{\mathrm{Cal,L}}(d)$, calibration status, calibration case, calibration size $n_{\mathrm{Cal}}$, bootstrap location sample $\{L_1^*(d),\ldots,L_B^*(d)\}$, chart parameters $CL_{\mathrm{CCSSBU-L-boot}}(d)$ and $UCL_{\mathrm{CCSSBU-L-boot}}(d)$, and OOC counts $OOC_{ND}(d)$, $OOC_{3A}(d)$, and $OOC_{3B}(d)$.

**Step 2. Define the location-shift grid and benchmark model.** Calculate the mean and empirical standard deviation of the Stage 3A USL-normalized observations as $\mu_0=\operatorname{mean}\left(\{Z_{ti}:e_t\in D_{3A}\}\right)$ and $s_Z=sd\left(\{Z_{ti}:e_t\in D_{3A}\}\right)$, respectively. To maintain a nondegenerate benchmark distribution and shift scale when the USL-normalized observations exhibit little or no variability, define $\sigma_Z=\max(s_Z,h_{\min})$, where $h_{\min}=0.05$ is the minimum smoothing bandwidth used in the d-CCSSBU chart construction algorithm. The resulting in-control benchmark model is $Z\sim N(\mu_0,\sigma_Z^2)$. Let $\rho$ denote a location-shift magnitude expressed in units of $\sigma_Z$ and define the out-of-control (OC) shift grid as $\Omega_\rho=\{0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0,2.5,3.0\}$. The corresponding additive shift on the USL-normalized residue scale is $\rho\sigma_Z$.

**Step 3. Estimate candidate-specific ARL$_1$ curves.** For each candidate value $d$ and shift value $\rho\in\Omega_\rho$, define $L_b^{*,\rho}(d)=L_b^*(d)+\rho\sigma_Z$ and estimate the OC signal probability as $p_1(d,\rho)=B^{-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}I\{L_b^*(d)+\rho\sigma_Z>UCL_{\mathrm{CCSSBU-L-boot}}(d)\}$. Estimate the corresponding average run length as $ARL_1(d,\rho)=1/p_1(d,\rho)$.

**Step 4. Evaluate benchmark ARL$_1$ performance.** For each shift value $\rho\in\Omega_\rho$, evaluate the conventional $\bar X$ chart benchmark under the same additive shift $\rho\sigma_Z$ on the USL-normalized residue scale. Define the OC process mean as $\mu_1(\rho)=\mu_0+\rho\sigma_Z$. For subgroup size $n$, the OC subgroup mean follows $\bar Z_t\sim N\left(\mu_1(\rho),\sigma_Z^2/n\right)$. Calibrate the one-sided UCL as $UCL_{\bar X}=\mu_0+\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha)\sigma_Z/\sqrt{n}$, where $\alpha=1/ARL_0$. Calculate the OC signal probability as $p_{1,\bar X}(\rho,n)=P\left(\bar Z_t>UCL_{\bar X}\mid\mu_1(\rho)\right)$ and the benchmark average run length as $ARL_{1,\bar X}(\rho,n)=1/p_{1,\bar X}(\rho,n)$.

**Step 5. Apply Rule 1 (ND-event protection).** Define $\mathcal D_1=\{d:OOC_{ND}(d)=0\}$.

**Step 6. Apply Rule 2 (Stage 3A protection).** Define $\mathcal D_2=\{d:OOC_{3A}(d)=0\}$. Construct the operationally admissible set $\mathcal A$ hierarchically as $\mathcal D_1\cap\mathcal D_2$ when nonempty; otherwise $\mathcal D_1$ when nonempty; otherwise $\mathcal D_2$ when nonempty; otherwise $\{1,\ldots,q\}$.

**Step 7. Apply Rule 3 (ARL$_1$ comparison).** For each candidate $d\in\mathcal A$ and shift value $\rho\in\Omega_\rho$, compute the relative ARL ratio $R(d,\rho)=ARL_1(d,\rho)/ARL_{1,\bar X}(\rho,n)$. Define the worst-case relative ARL ratio as $W(d)=\max_{\rho\in\Omega_\rho}R(d,\rho)$ and the geometric mean relative ARL ratio as $G(d)=\exp\{|\Omega_\rho|^{-1}\sum_{\rho\in\Omega_\rho}\log R(d,\rho)\}$. Define the benchmark-superior set as $\mathcal U=\{d\in\mathcal A:W(d)\le1\}$.

**Step 8. Recommend value of $d$.** Two ARL$_1$ comparison cases are considered.

**U Case:** $\mathcal U\neq\varnothing$. At least one operationally admissible candidate remains benchmark-superior throughout the complete shift grid. Select $d_{\mathrm{rec}}=\max\mathcal U$ according to Rule 3.

**XO Case:** $\mathcal U=\varnothing$. No operationally admissible candidate remains benchmark-superior throughout the complete shift grid. Select the preliminary recommendation as $d_{\mathrm{rec}}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{d\in\mathcal A}W(d)$. If multiple candidates attain the same minimum value of $W(d)$, select the candidate with the smallest value of $G(d)$. If a tie still remains, select the largest value of $d$ according to Rule 3.

The decision path is classified into one of the following eight cases.

**Case 1:** $\mathcal A=\mathcal D_1\cap\mathcal D_2$ and U Case.

**Case 2:** $\mathcal A=\mathcal D_1\cap\mathcal D_2$ and XO Case.

**Case 3:** $\mathcal A=\mathcal D_1$ and U Case.

**Case 4:** $\mathcal A=\mathcal D_1$ and XO Case.

**Case 5:** $\mathcal A=\mathcal D_2$ and U Case.

**Case 6:** $\mathcal A=\mathcal D_2$ and XO Case.

**Case 7:** $\mathcal A=\{1,\ldots,q\}$ and U Case.

**Case 8:** $\mathcal A=\{1,\ldots,q\}$ and XO Case.

Apply Steps 1--8 separately to DAR, CAR, and Mic. Report the corresponding values of $s_Z$ and $\sigma_Z$ together with the resulting recommendations as $d_{\mathrm{DAR}}$, $d_{\mathrm{CAR}}$, and $d_{\mathrm{Mic}}$.


### Selection of $d$ for the d-CCSSBU-S Chart {#sec-d-select-s}

For a given residue type, such as DAR, the following procedure evaluates candidate values of $d$ under multiplicative increases in process variability and recommends a preferred value of $d$.

**Step 1. Construct d-specific d-CCSSBU-S charts.** Apply the d-CCSSBU-S chart construction algorithm in @sec-dccssbu-s-algorithm for each candidate value $d\in\{1,\ldots,q\}$. For each candidate $d$, obtain $D_{\mathrm{Cal,S}}(d)$, calibration status, calibration case, calibration size $n_{\mathrm{Cal}}$, bootstrap scale sample $\{S_1^*(d),\ldots,S_B^*(d)\}$, chart parameters $CL_{\mathrm{CCSSBU-S-boot}}(d)$ and $UCL_{\mathrm{CCSSBU-S-boot}}(d)$, and OOC counts $OOC_{ND}(d)$, $OOC_{3A}(d)$, and $OOC_{3B}(d)$.

**Step 2. Define the variability-ratio grid and benchmark model.** Calculate the mean and empirical standard deviation of the Stage 3A USL-normalized observations as $\mu_0=\operatorname{mean}\left(\{Z_{ti}:e_t\in D_{3A}\}\right)$ and $s_Z=sd\left(\{Z_{ti}:e_t\in D_{3A}\}\right)$, respectively. To maintain a nondegenerate benchmark distribution when the USL-normalized observations exhibit little or no variability, define $\sigma_Z=\max(s_Z,h_{\min})$, where $h_{\min}=0.05$ is the minimum smoothing bandwidth used in the d-CCSSBU chart construction algorithm. The resulting in-control benchmark model is $Z\sim N(\mu_0,\sigma_Z^2)$. Let $\rho$ denote the multiplicative variability ratio and define the OC variability-ratio grid as $\Omega_\rho=\{1.05,1.10,1.20,1.50,2.00,2.25\}$.

**Step 3. Estimate candidate-specific ARL$_1$ curves.** For each candidate value $d$ and variability ratio $\rho\in\Omega_\rho$, define the shifted bootstrap scale statistic as $S_b^{*,\rho}(d)=\rho S_b^*(d)$. Estimate the OC signal probability as $p_1(d,\rho)=B^{-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}I\{\rho S_b^*(d)>UCL_{\mathrm{CCSSBU-S-boot}}(d)\}$ and estimate the corresponding average run length as $ARL_1(d,\rho)=1/p_1(d,\rho)$.

**Step 4. Evaluate benchmark ARL$_1$ performance.** For each variability ratio $\rho\in\Omega_\rho$, evaluate the conventional $S$ chart benchmark under the same multiplicative increase in process variability. Define the OC process standard deviation as $\sigma_1(\rho)=\rho\sigma_Z$. Assuming normality and subgroup size $n$, the subgroup standard deviation satisfies $(n-1)S_t^2/\sigma_1^2(\rho)\sim\chi^2_{n-1}$. Calibrate the IC one-sided upper control limit as $UCL_S=\sigma_Z\sqrt{\chi^2_{1-\alpha,n-1}/(n-1)}$, where $\alpha=1/ARL_0$ and $\chi^2_{1-\alpha,n-1}$ denotes the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of the chi-squared distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom. Calculate the OC signal probability as $p_{1,S}(\rho,n)=P\left(S_t>UCL_S\mid\sigma_1(\rho)\right)$ and the benchmark average run length as $ARL_{1,S}(\rho,n)=1/p_{1,S}(\rho,n)$.

**Step 5. Apply Rule 1 (ND-event protection).** Define $\mathcal D_1=\{d:OOC_{ND}(d)=0\}$.

**Step 6. Apply Rule 2 (Stage 3A protection).** Define $\mathcal D_2=\{d:OOC_{3A}(d)=0\}$. Construct the operationally admissible set $\mathcal A$ hierarchically as $\mathcal D_1\cap\mathcal D_2$ when nonempty; otherwise $\mathcal D_1$ when nonempty; otherwise $\mathcal D_2$ when nonempty; otherwise $\{1,\ldots,q\}$.

**Step 7. Apply Rule 3 (ARL$_1$ comparison).** For each candidate $d\in\mathcal A$ and variability ratio $\rho\in\Omega_\rho$, compute the relative ARL ratio $R(d,\rho)=ARL_1(d,\rho)/ARL_{1,S}(\rho,n)$. Define the worst-case relative ARL ratio as $W(d)=\max_{\rho\in\Omega_\rho}R(d,\rho)$ and the geometric mean relative ARL ratio as $G(d)=\exp\{|\Omega_\rho|^{-1}\sum_{\rho\in\Omega_\rho}\log R(d,\rho)\}$. Define the benchmark-superior set as $\mathcal U=\{d\in\mathcal A:W(d)\le1\}$.

**Step 8. Recommend a value of $d$.** Two ARL$_1$ comparison cases are considered.

**U Case:** $\mathcal U\neq\varnothing$. At least one operationally admissible candidate remains benchmark-superior throughout the complete variability-ratio grid. Select $d_{\mathrm{rec}}=\max\mathcal U$ according to Rule 3.

**XO Case:** $\mathcal U=\varnothing$. No operationally admissible candidate remains benchmark-superior throughout the complete variability-ratio grid. Select $d_{\mathrm{rec}}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{d\in\mathcal A}W(d)$. If multiple candidates attain the same minimum value of $W(d)$, select the candidate with the smallest value of $G(d)$. If a tie still remains, select the largest value of $d$ according to Rule 3.

The decision path is classified into one of the following eight cases.

**Case 1:** $\mathcal A=\mathcal D_1\cap\mathcal D_2$ and U Case.

**Case 2:** $\mathcal A=\mathcal D_1\cap\mathcal D_2$ and XO Case.

**Case 3:** $\mathcal A=\mathcal D_1$ and U Case.

**Case 4:** $\mathcal A=\mathcal D_1$ and XO Case.

**Case 5:** $\mathcal A=\mathcal D_2$ and U Case.

**Case 6:** $\mathcal A=\mathcal D_2$ and XO Case.

**Case 7:** $\mathcal A=\{1,\ldots,q\}$ and U Case.

**Case 8:** $\mathcal A=\{1,\ldots,q\}$ and XO Case.

Apply Steps 1--8 separately to DAR, CAR, and Mic. Report the resulting recommendations as $d_{\mathrm{DAR}}$, $d_{\mathrm{CAR}}$, and $d_{\mathrm{Mic}}$. 

### Interpretation of Recommended Heterogeneity Indices

The d-CCSSBU-L and d-CCSSBU-S charts implement the knowledge-driven and risk-based cluster-calibration framework for location and scale monitoring, respectively. Because location and scale represent distinct dimensions of process stability, the optimal heterogeneity index for location monitoring, denoted by $d_L$, need not equal the optimal heterogeneity index for scale monitoring, denoted by $d_S$. 

The recommended values $d_L$ and $d_S$ represent the numbers of highest-risk ordered clusters retained in the calibration sets used for location and scale chart construction, respectively. Smaller values focus calibration on a narrower collection of highest-risk clusters, whereas larger values incorporate greater process heterogeneity into the calibration structure. The recommended values are determined through ND-event protection, Stage 3A-event protection, and benchmark-referenced OOC detection performance and heterogeneity-retention criteria described above.

Consequently, the recommended values of $d_L$ and $d_S$ should be interpreted as the largest amounts of cluster heterogeneity that can be incorporated into chart calibration while remaining consistent with ND-event protection, Stage 3A protection where feasible,  and benchmark-referenced OOC detection performance.

## Chart-Selection Algorithm for Mic Data: Poisson $u$ Chart or d-CCSSBU Charts {#sec-poisson}

Unlike DAR and CAR measurements, Mic observations are nonnegative count data and share a common microbial USL. When microbial results are reported below a microbial detection limit (e.g., <1 CFU/swab), they are converted to count values according to the site's microbiological reporting convention before analysis. Count data are often appropriately modeled by the Poisson distribution, and extensive literature exists on the statistical analysis and capability assessment of Poisson processes [@Poisson2016; @Discrete2023; @Anscombe1948; @Freeman1950]. Therefore, a Poisson $u$ chart is preferred when the Mic process is compatible with the Poisson distribution. When the Poisson assumption is not supported by the data, d-CCSSBU-L and d-CCSSBU-S charts are applied instead.

For cleaning event $e_t$, let $X_{ti}$ denote the microbial count at sampling location $i$ and let $p_t$ denote the number of observed sampling locations. Missing observations are excluded, and each observed sampling location is treated as one comparable exposure unit because all results use the same CFU/swab basis.

**Step 1. Calculate event-level microbial statistics.** For event $e_t$, calculate the total microbial count as $Y_t=\sum_{i=1}^{p_t}X_{ti}$ and the microbial density as $u_t=Y_t/p_t$. For display on the common percentage-of-USL scale, calculate $u_t^*=100u_t/\mathrm{USL}$. Conduct all Poisson-model assessments using the original integer counts $X_{ti}$ rather than the normalized values.

**Step 2. Create nominal Stage 3A and Stage 3B datasets.** If $x= n_{3A}$, define $D_{\mathrm{3A}}=\{e_1,\ldots,e_x\}$ and $D_{\mathrm{3B}}=\emptyset$. If $x>n_{3A}$, define $D_{\mathrm{3A}}=\{e_1,\ldots,e_{n_{3A}}\}$ and $D_{\mathrm{3B}}=\{e_{n_{3A}+1},\ldots,e_x\}$.

**Step 3. Select the Poisson-assessment dataset.** Apply one of the following data-availability cases.

**Case 1: All available counts are zero.** If all available Mic counts are zeros, do not construct a Poisson $u$ chart because $\hat\lambda=0$ produces a degenerate center line and upper control limits. Apply the d-CCSSBU-L and d-CCSSBU-S charts. Unlike the Poisson $u$ chart, the CCSSB calibration procedure incorporates smoothing with a positive minimum bandwidth and therefore remains applicable even when all observed counts are identical.

**Case 2: Stage 3A counts are zero and Stage 3B contains a positive count.** If all Stage 3A counts are zero but at least one Stage 3B count is positive, use all available Mic observations as the Poisson-assessment dataset. The resulting chart parameters are estimated from all currently available observations and retained for monitoring of future events.

**Case 3: Stage 3A contains a positive count.** If Stage 3A contains at least one positive Mic count, use the Stage 3A observations as the Poisson-assessment and calibration dataset. Reserve Stage 3B events for monitoring when the Poisson $u$ chart is selected.

**Step 4. Estimate the Poisson rate.** Using the dataset selected in Step 3, estimate the microbial rate per sampled location as $\hat\lambda=\sum_tY_t/\sum_tp_t$. Under the Poisson model, each individual count satisfies $X_{ti}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$, with $E(X_{ti})=\mathrm{Var}(X_{ti})=\lambda$.

**Step 5. Assess Poisson goodness of fit.** Calculate a Pearson-type goodness-of-fit statistic from the individual microbial counts. Generate parametric bootstrap datasets from $\mathrm{Poisson}(\hat\lambda)$ using the same number of observations as the assessment dataset, recalculate the statistic for each bootstrap dataset, and estimate the goodness-of-fit p-value as the proportion of bootstrap statistics at least as large as the observed statistic. Classify the Poisson goodness-of-fit condition as satisfied when the bootstrap p-value exceeds the prespecified significance level $\alpha_{\mathrm{GOF}}$.

**Step 6. Assess overdispersion.** Calculate the dispersion ratio as $\phi=s_X^2/\bar X$, where $\bar X$ and $s_X^2$ are the sample mean and sample variance of the individual counts in the Poisson-assessment dataset. Evaluate overdispersion using the prespecified bootstrap or analytical criterion implemented in the analysis. Classify the no- stepsubstantial-overdispersion condition as satisfied when the observed dispersion is not significantly greater than that expected under $\mathrm{Poisson}(\hat\lambda)$.

**Step 7. Select the Mic charting method.** Select the Poisson $u$ chart when the assessment dataset contains at least one positive count, the Poisson goodness-of-fit condition is satisfied, and no substantial overdispersion is detected. Otherwise, select the d-CCSSBU-L and d-CCSSBU-S charts.

Under an accepted Poisson model, a separate scale chart is unnecessary because the mean and variance are both governed by $\lambda$. When the Poisson model is unsupported, the d-CCSSBU charts monitor location and scale separately without requiring a count-distribution assumption.

**Step 8. Construct the Poisson $u$ chart when selected.** Use the Poisson calibration dataset selected in Step 3 to estimate the center line as $\bar u=\sum_tY_t/\sum_tp_t$. Express the center line on the normalized scale as $CL_u^*=100\bar u/\mathrm{USL}$.

For event $e_t$, calculate the exact one-sided Poisson upper control limit for the total count as $UCL_{Y,t}=q_{1-\alpha}\{\mathrm{Poisson}(p_t\bar u)\}$, where $\alpha=1/\mathrm{ARL}_0$ and $q_{1-\alpha}$ denotes the corresponding Poisson quantile. Calculate the event-specific density limit as $UCL_{u,t}=UCL_{Y,t}/p_t$ and its normalized value as $UCL_{u,t}^*=100UCL_{u,t}/\mathrm{USL}$. In this study, $\mathrm{ARL}_0=740$ and therefore $\alpha=1/740$.

Plot $\{u_1^*,u_2^*,\ldots,u_x^*\}$ against cleaning-event order together with $CL_u^*$ and the event-specific limits $\{UCL_{u,1}^*,UCL_{u,2}^*,\ldots,UCL_{u,x}^*\}$. Classify event $e_t$ as potentially out-of-control when $u_t^*>UCL_{u,t}^*$. A lower control limit is not used because decreases in microbial counts represent improved rather than adverse cleaning performance.

Under Case 3, retain the Stage 3A rate estimate and control limits for Stage 3B monitoring. Under Case 2, estimate the chart parameters using all currently available observations and retain the resulting parameters for monitoring of future events.


**Step 9. Construct d-CCSSBU charts when selected.** The d-CCSSBU-L chart monitors the event-level median of the normalized Mic observations, whereas the d-CCSSBU-S chart monitors their event-level MAD. Apply these charts to all-zero datasets, datasets that do not support the Poisson model, or datasets exhibiting substantial overdispersion.

**Comments.** \textcolor{blue}{The algorithm used the exact Poisson $u$ chart, which has a discrete upper control limit derived from the exact Poisson distribution. A conventional $3\sigma$ Poisson $u$ chart uses the same monitoring statistic but approximates the upper control limit by $UCL_t=\bar u_t+3\sqrt{\frac{\bar u_t}{n_t}},$ where $\bar u_t$ is the estimated average nonconformity rate (and equals $\bar \mu_t^*$  in Step 8) and $n_t$ is the inspection opportunity associated with the $t$th event. Because the exact Poisson $u$ chart accounts for the discrete Poisson distribution directly, differences between the exact and $3\sigma$ limits can occur, especially when $\bar u_t$ or $n_t$ is small as in CV data.}


## Recalibration or Retraining {#sec-recalibration}

Recalibration or retraining is performed when the current Stage 3A calibration dataset is no longer considered representative of the current cleaning process. Examples include process changes, equipment modifications, cleaning-procedure revisions, analytical-method changes, newly available validation information, or sustained process improvement.

A new representative Stage 3A dataset containing $n_{3A}$ eligible cleaning events is selected and ordered chronologically as $D_{\mathrm{3A}}=\{e_1,e_2,\ldots,e_{n_{3A}}\}$. The eligible-event sequence $D$ is then updated and the corresponding chart-construction and chart-selection procedures are reapplied.

For the d-CCSSBU-L chart, rerun the chart-construction algorithm and the d-selection procedure to obtain updated chart parameters and, when applicable, an updated recommended value $d_L$. 

For the d-CCSSBU-S chart, rerun the chart-construction algorithm and the d-selection procedure to obtain updated chart parameters and, when applicable, an updated recommended value $d_S$. 

For Mic data monitored using a Poisson $u$ chart, repeat the chart-selection algorithm using the updated calibration dataset. If the Poisson model remains supported, re-estimate the microbial count rate and the corresponding control limits. Otherwise, monitor the Mic data using the d-CCSSBU-L and d-CCSSBU-S charts.

Because residue observations are expressed relative to their corresponding acceptance criteria through USL normalization, historically collected CV observations may be placed on a common scale when the underlying equipment, cleaning process, analytical methodology, and acceptance criteria remain scientifically comparable. This property facilitates recalibration or retraining using information accumulated across different time periods, products, or validation studies.

# Results

Applications of the proposed algorithms and methodologies to the Equipment A and Equipment B case studies are presented in this section.

## Selection of $d$ for the d-CCSSBU-L Chart

The d-selection algorithm  was applied to Equipment A and Equipment B to identify the recommended heterogeneity index $d$ for each residue type DAR, CAR, and Mic. The resulting recommendations and corresponding ARL$_1$ performance profiles are presented below.


```{r d-ccssbu-l-function}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

d_ccssbu_l <- function(file,
                       equipment_label = "Equipment A",
                       residue_type = "DAR",
                       sheet = residue_type,

                       # d-CCSSBU-L design parameters
                       d = 3,
                       n_stage3A_events = 10,
                       target_ARL0 = 740,
                       B = 20000,
                       c_smooth = 0.5,
                       h_min = 0.05,
                       seed = 123,

                       # Location-calibration eligibility and distinct-L_t control
                       location_eligibility_threshold = 70,
                       location_distinct_digits = 10,

                       # Cluster definition
                       cluster_col = "USL",
                       cluster_group_cols = NULL,
                       cluster_round_digits = 10,

                       # Input columns
                       event_col = "Event",
                       location_col = "Location",
                       result_col = "Result",
                       lod_col = "LOD",
                       loq_col = "LOQ",
                       usl_col = "USL",

                       # Output controls
                       plot_chart = TRUE,
                       save_outputs = TRUE,
                       output_dir = file.path(getwd(), "d_CCSSBU_L_Charts"),
                       return_bootstrap_matrix = FALSE,
                       keep_bootstrap_statistics = TRUE) {

  required_pkgs <- c(
    "readxl",
    "dplyr",
    "ggplot2",
    "stringr",
    "readr",
    "matrixStats"
  )

  missing_pkgs <- required_pkgs[
    !(required_pkgs %in% rownames(installed.packages()))
  ]

  if (length(missing_pkgs) > 0) {
    stop(
      "Please install the following package(s): ",
      paste(missing_pkgs, collapse = ", ")
    )
  }

  library(readxl)
  library(dplyr)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(stringr)
  library(readr)
  library(matrixStats)

  if (target_ARL0 <= 1) {
    stop("target_ARL0 must be greater than 1.")
  }

  if (B <= 0) {
    stop("B must be positive.")
  }

  if (d < 1) {
    stop("d must be a positive integer.")
  }

  if (n_stage3A_events < 1) {
    stop("n_stage3A_events must be a positive integer.")
  }

  if (c_smooth < 0) {
    stop("c_smooth must be nonnegative.")
  }

  if (h_min < 0) {
    stop("h_min must be nonnegative.")
  }

  if (location_eligibility_threshold <= 0) {
    stop("location_eligibility_threshold must be positive.")
  }

  if (save_outputs && !dir.exists(output_dir)) {
    dir.create(output_dir, recursive = TRUE)
  }

  set.seed(seed)

  alpha <- 1 / target_ARL0

  # ------------------------------------------------------------
  # Helper functions
  # ------------------------------------------------------------

  mad_unscaled <- function(x) {
    x <- x[!is.na(x) & is.finite(x)]

    if (length(x) == 0) {
      return(NA_real_)
    }

    med_x <- median(x, na.rm = TRUE)

    median(
      abs(x - med_x),
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  }

  is_nd_result <- function(x) {
    x_chr <- trimws(toupper(as.character(x)))

    x_chr %in% c(
      "ND",
      "N.D.",
      "N/D",
      "NON-DETECT",
      "NONDETECT",
      "NON DETECT",
      "NOT DETECT"
    )
  }

  extract_event_number <- function(x) {
    x_chr <- trimws(as.character(x))

    x_num_direct <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x_chr))

    x_num_extracted <- suppressWarnings(
      as.numeric(stringr::str_extract(x_chr, "\\d+$"))
    )

    dplyr::case_when(
      !is.na(x_num_direct) ~ x_num_direct,
      !is.na(x_num_extracted) ~ x_num_extracted,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    )
  }

  fast_quantile <- function(x, probs) {
    x <- x[!is.na(x) & is.finite(x)]

    if (length(x) == 0) {
      return(NA_real_)
    }

    as.numeric(
      stats::quantile(
        x = x,
        probs = probs,
        na.rm = TRUE,
        type = 7,
        names = FALSE
      )
    )
  }

  safe_name <- function(x) {
    gsub(
      pattern = "[^A-Za-z0-9]+",
      replacement = "_",
      x = as.character(x)
    )
  }

  safe_plot_text <- function(x) {
    x <- as.character(x)
    x <- gsub("_", "-", x)
    x
  }

  # ------------------------------------------------------------
  # Read data
  # ------------------------------------------------------------

  all_sheets <- readxl::excel_sheets(file)

  if (!(sheet %in% all_sheets)) {
    stop(
      "Requested sheet was not found: ",
      sheet,
      ". Available sheets: ",
      paste(all_sheets, collapse = ", ")
    )
  }

  message("d-CCSSBU-L equipment = ", equipment_label)
  message("Residue type = ", residue_type)
  message("Sheet used = ", sheet)
  message("Cluster column = ", cluster_col)
  message(
    "d = ", d,
    "; n_stage3A_events = ", n_stage3A_events,
    "; target ARL0 = ", target_ARL0,
    "; alpha = ", signif(alpha, 5),
    "; B = ", B,
    "; c_smooth = ", c_smooth,
    "; h_min = ", h_min,
    "; location eligibility threshold = ", location_eligibility_threshold,
    "; seed = ", seed
  )

  dat_raw <- readxl::read_excel(
    path = file,
    sheet = sheet
  )

  dat_raw <- dat_raw %>%
    dplyr::rename_with(~ stringr::str_trim(.x))

  result_col_actual <- result_col

  if (!(result_col_actual %in% names(dat_raw)) && residue_type %in% names(dat_raw)) {
    result_col_actual <- residue_type
  }

  required_cols <- c(
    event_col,
    location_col,
    result_col_actual,
    lod_col,
    loq_col,
    usl_col,
    cluster_col
  )

  if (!is.null(cluster_group_cols)) {
    required_cols <- c(required_cols, cluster_group_cols)
  }

  missing_cols <- setdiff(
    required_cols,
    names(dat_raw)
  )

  if (length(missing_cols) > 0) {
    stop(
```
