\textcolor{blue}{Taken together, the genuine-data analysis, the independent-location simulation, and the correlated-location simulation produced a consistent finding for the location statistic. Across all investigated settings, the location-stratified bootstrap yielded location-chart control limits that were either comparable to or more conservative than those obtained from event-level resampling. In contrast, the scale-statistic results were less consistent. Depending on the data structure, the location-stratified bootstrap could produce either smaller or larger scale control limits than the event-level approach. This behavior was particularly evident in data containing substantial nondetect observations, ties, and zero-MAD events. These findings suggest that the principal effect of location-stratified bootstrap resampling is on the estimation of scale-related limits rather than location-related limits. Because the location chart serves as the primary monitoring tool in the proposed framework, the consistent conservativeness of $UCL_{L,\mathrm{loc}}$ supports the practical use of location-stratified bootstrapping when only a limited number of complete cleaning events are available. The scale chart should be interpreted as a supplementary diagnostic tool, with any out-of-control signal followed by additional investigation using location-level comparisons, variance-component assessment, or related analyses to identify the underlying source of process variation.}


**Why $n_{3A}=10$?** In [@Montgomery2020; @Qiu2014spc; @Chakraborti2019], \textcolor{blue}{many Phase I control-chart examples contain approximately 20--30 subgroups (points), although examples with fewer than 20 subgroups are also presented. However, to the authors' knowledge, there is no dedicated reference specifying a minimum number of control-chart points for pharmaceutical manufacturing process validation or cleaning process validation.}

\textcolor{blue}{From a practical GMP perspective, stability assessment should begin as early as reasonably possible rather than be postponed until a substantially larger dataset becomes available. This consideration is particularly important for cleaning validation, for which data are typically sparse and accumulate slowly over time. Moreover, the data requirement in the proposed multicluster framework differs from that of conventional one-cluster SPC. With $d$ clusters and a Stage 3A requirement of $n_{3A}$ observations per cluster, approximately $d n_{3A}$ events are required. Consequently, setting $n_{3A}=30$, for example, could require approximately $30d$ events before prospective monitoring begins. For sparse cleaning-validation data, such a requirement could substantially delay the implementation of prospective monitoring and reduce its practical value.}

\textcolor{blue}{Therefore, $n_{3A}=10$ was selected as a provisional minimum Stage 3A requirement, rather than as a theoretically optimal sample size. The purpose is to balance statistical reliability with the practical need to initiate stability assessment and prospective monitoring with the available data.}

\textcolor{blue}{The ARL$_1$ results for Equipment A provide additional empirical support for this choice. As shown in} @fig-d-selection-curve-a-l and @fig-d-selection-curve-a-s, \textcolor{blue}{the proposed charts constructed with $n_{3A}=10$ do not exhibit a general deterioration in shift-detection performance relative to the conventional $\bar{X}$- and $S$-chart ARL$_1$ benchmarks. Rather, the relative performance depends on the residue type and the magnitude of the process change. Notably, for DAR in} @fig-d-selection-curve-a-l, \textcolor{blue}{the proposed chart yields lower ARL$_1$ values than the conventional $\bar{X}$-chart benchmark over the evaluated shifts, indicating faster detection under those conditions. In other comparisons, the conventional benchmark may perform better. Thus, neither approach uniformly dominates the other across the evaluated conditions. These results demonstrate that the practical choice of $n_{3A}=10$ does not inherently compromise the detection capability of the proposed multicluster charts relative to conventional SPC benchmarks.}

\textcolor{blue}{Nevertheless, $n_{3A}=10$ should be interpreted as a minimum starting requirement, not as the statistically preferred sample size when more data are available. As observations accumulate, practitioners are strongly encouraged to increase $n_{3A}$ toward the commonly used range of 20--30 observations per cluster, or to follow statistically justified sample-size recommendations that consider Type I error, Type II error, estimation reliability, and the practical time required for data accumulation.}


**Why 100% of the USL?** \textcolor{blue}{The 100\% USL threshold used for calibration-event selection corresponds directly to the established specification limit. Under GMP requirements, conformance to established specifications is required for product acceptance, and failure to meet an established specification constitutes an out-of-specification (OOS) result that requires appropriate investigation. Therefore, only observations satisfying $X \le \mathrm{USL}$ are eligible for inclusion in calibration-event selection. Equivalently, under USL normalization, $R = 100\frac{X}{\mathrm{USL}},$ the eligibility criterion is simply $R \le 100\%.$ Thus, the 100\% threshold is not an additional statistical restriction or a tuning parameter introduced by the proposed method. Rather, it represents the existing specification boundary and allows all within-specification observations to remain eligible for calibration-event selection.}
 
**Impact of ND Replacement by LOD or LOQ.** \textcolor{blue}{With an assumption of a known distribution,} [@Walsh2022a; @Walsh2022b] \textcolor{blue}{and references therein discuss the influence of different proportions of ND observations on location and scale statistics when ND observations are replaced by a constant. In general, replacing ND observations with a common upper-bound value tends to increase estimated location statistics while reducing estimated variability when many observations are assigned the same replacement value. Consequently, event-level location and scale statistics and the resulting control limits may differ from those that would be obtained if the true unobserved values were known.}

\textcolor{blue}{However, the distribution of CV data is generally unknown. In this study, ND observations are replaced by the LOD, or by the LOQ when the LOD is unavailable, before application of the proposed method. This is a conservative practice consistent with the pharmaceutical worst-case principle when the exact value is unavailable. We accept this commonly used and convenient practice as an upstream data-handling procedure rather than proposing it as part of the control-chart methodology. The objective of this study is to develop a distribution-free control-chart framework that can handle the resulting mixed discrete-continuous data, rather than to develop an imputation method for censored observations.}

\textcolor{blue}{Ties resulting from constant replacement of ND observations do not prevent application of the proposed method, and zero or very small MAD values are accommodated by the predefined scale floor, $\sigma_t=\max(s_t,0.05)$. If another scientifically justified method is used to handle ND observations, the resulting data can simply be supplied to the same control-chart algorithm.}

\textcolor{blue}{To further examine monitoring performance under different levels of ND prevalence,} @tbl-equipment-ab-nd-event-summary \textcolor{blue}{summarizes the proportions of ND events in the DAR and CAR datasets for Equipment A and Equipment B.  The four datasets represent markedly different ND-event proportions: 10.00\% for Equipment A DAR, 100.00\% for Equipment A CAR, 74.00\% for Equipment B DAR, and 84.62\% for Equipment B CAR. Thus, the empirical evaluation includes datasets ranging from relatively low ND prevalence to predominantly ND observations.}

\textcolor{blue}{The corresponding ARL$_1$ results in} @fig-d-selection-curve-a-l, @fig-d-selection-curve-b-l, @fig-d-selection-curve-a-s, and @fig-d-selection-curve-b-s \textcolor{blue}{provide empirical evidence regarding detection performance under these different ND conditions. For Equipment A DAR, which contained 10.00\% ND events, the d-CCSSBU-L chart showed lower ARL$_1$ than the conventional $\bar{X}$-chart benchmark over the evaluated shifts, while the d-CCSSBU-S chart did not show a uniform disadvantage relative to the conventional $S$ chart. For Equipment A CAR, in which all 10 events were ND events, the d-CCSSBU-L chart did not show a general sensitivity disadvantage relative to the $\bar{X}$ chart, whereas the d-CCSSBU-S chart showed poorer ARL$_1$ performance than the conventional $S$ chart. For Equipment B DAR and CAR, which contained 74.00\% and 84.62\% ND events, respectively, neither the proposed charts nor the corresponding conventional benchmarks uniformly dominated across the evaluated shifts.}

\textcolor{blue}{Taken together, these results show that the proposed charts remain applicable across datasets having substantially different ND-event proportions and do not exhibit systematically inferior detection performance relative to the conventional $\bar{X}$- and $S$-chart benchmarks. At the same time, the results also demonstrate that substantial ND prevalence and the ties induced by constant LOD/LOQ replacement can affect detection sensitivity, particularly for the scale statistic. Therefore, the results should not be interpreted as showing that ND replacement has no effect. Rather, they indicate that the proposed framework can remain practically informative under substantial ND prevalence while the magnitude and direction of the sensitivity effect depend on the data structure, chart statistic, and process shift. Different ND proportions, reporting limits, or alternative ND-handling procedures may further affect the resulting event-level statistics and control limits. ND handling and subsequent control-chart construction are therefore treated as separate analytical issues in this study.}



```{r}
#| label: tbl-equipment-ab-nd-event-summary
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis
#| tbl-cap: "Numbers and proportions of ND and non-ND events for Equipment A and Equipment B."

library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

summarize_nd_events <- function(
    file,
    equipment_label,
    sheets = c("DAR", "CAR"),
    event_col = "Event",
    result_col = "Result") {

  purrr::map_dfr(
    sheets,
    function(sheet_i) {

      data_i <- readxl::read_excel(
        path = file,
        sheet = sheet_i
      ) |>
        dplyr::filter(
          !is.na(.data[[event_col]]),
          !is.na(.data[[result_col]])
        )

      event_tbl <- data_i |>
        dplyr::group_by(
          Event = .data[[event_col]]
        ) |>
        dplyr::summarise(
          n_distinct_results =
            dplyr::n_distinct(.data[[result_col]]),
          ND_event =
            n_distinct_results == 1,
          .groups = "drop"
        )

      n_total <- nrow(event_tbl)
      n_ND <- sum(event_tbl$ND_event)
      n_non_ND <- n_total - n_ND

      tibble::tibble(
        Equipment = equipment_label,
        Residue = sheet_i,
        `Total events` = n_total,
        `ND events` = n_ND,
        `Non-ND events` = n_non_ND,
        `ND (%)` = 100 * n_ND / n_total,
        `Non-ND (%)` = 100 * n_non_ND / n_total
      )
    }
  )
}

# Equipment A and B
equipment_ab_nd_summary <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  summarize_nd_events(
    file = file,
    equipment_label = "Equipment A"
  ),
  summarize_nd_events(
    file = file1,
    equipment_label = "Equipment B"
  )
) |>
  dplyr::arrange(
    Equipment,
    Residue
  )

# One combined table
equipment_ab_nd_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "latex",
    booktabs = TRUE,
    digits = 2,
    align = c(
      "l", "l", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c"
    ),
    escape = TRUE
  ) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    latex_options = c(
      "hold_position",
      "scale_down"
    ),
    position = "center",
    font_size = 8
  ) |>
  cat()
```

**Mixed Stage 3A/3B Status of Multicluster Control Charts.** \textcolor{blue}{The proposed Stage 3A/3B framework is designed for prospective application and can be implemented as a real-time monitoring system. Retrospective analysis can also be accommodated as a special application of this framework, as described in the algorithm. Accordingly, the Equipment A case study is a retrospective analysis because no subsequent Stage 3B observations are available. In contrast, the Equipment B case study is used to evaluate prospective Stage 3A/3B monitoring.}

\textcolor{blue}{The Equipment B data were accumulated through routine manufacturing activities and therefore were already historical when this study was conducted. To evaluate the proposed prospective procedure, however, the original time order was preserved and the data were intentionally partitioned according to time. Earlier $n_{3A}$ events were used for Stage 3A calibration, and subsequent events were sequentially evaluated according to the Stage 3B monitoring procedure. Thus, the Equipment B analysis represents a prospective monitoring analysis applied to retrospectively available, time-ordered data rather than a real-time prospective data collection study.}

\textcolor{blue}{Ideally, after Stage 3A is completed, the resulting reference UCL is finalized and subsequent Stage 3B location or scale statistics are sequentially monitored against this reference limit. However, the transition is more complex for a multicluster $d$-CCSSBU chart because the Stage 3A requirements may be satisfied at different times for different clusters. At an intermediate point, $l$ clusters may have completed their Stage 3A requirements and entered Stage 3B monitoring, while the remaining $d-l$ clusters are still in Stage 3A. We refer to this intermediate condition as the mixed Stage 3A/3B status of a multicluster control chart.}

\textcolor{blue}{During this mixed status, the $d-l$ clusters remaining in Stage 3A continue to contribute new calibration information. Consequently, the reference UCL for the overall multicluster chart remains provisional and may be updated as additional Stage 3A information becomes available. In contrast, subsequent events from the $l$ clusters that have completed Stage 3A are prospectively evaluated against the currently available UCL and are not used to estimate or update that UCL. Thus, events from the $d-l$ Stage 3A clusters have a calibration role, whereas subsequent events from the $l$ Stage 3B clusters have a monitoring role. Although Stage 3B monitoring has therefore begun for the $l$ completed clusters, the overall multicluster chart remains in a mixed Stage 3A/3B status because its reference UCL is still subject to updating from the remaining Stage 3A clusters.}

\textcolor{blue}{This procedure continues until the Stage 3A requirements have been satisfied for all $d$ selected clusters. At that point, Stage 3A calibration of the entire multicluster chart is complete, the reference UCL is finalized, and the chart enters full Stage 3B prospective monitoring. The multiple intermediate cases described in the algorithm therefore represent this mixed Stage 3A/3B transition, in which calibration and prospective monitoring occur simultaneously across different clusters, rather than a fully established Stage 3B state for the entire multicluster chart.}

**Why USL-Normalization Rather Than Standardization?** A fundamental objective of cleaning-validation analysis is comparison of observations generated under different residue acceptance criteria. Standardization using sample means and standard deviations removes location and scale differences statistically, but it does not preserve the regulatory interpretation of the resulting values relative to their acceptance criteria. For example, a residue measurement of 5 with a USL of 4 represents an out-of-specification (OOS) result, whereas the same measurement of 5 with a USL of 10 remains acceptable. After standardization, this distinction may no longer be apparent because the resulting standardized values depend on the sample mean and standard deviation rather than the applicable acceptance criterion. Consequently, standardization may obscure the compliance margin associated with the original observation. In contrast, USL-normalization expresses each observation as a percentage of its corresponding acceptance criterion and therefore preserves the regulatory interpretation of the result. In the preceding example, the two observations become $(5/4)\times100=125$ and $(5/10)\times100=50$, respectively. The USL-normalized values immediately indicate that the first observation exceeds its acceptance criterion whereas the second remains well below its acceptance criterion. Thus, USL-normalization preserves information regarding compliance status and compliance margin that is directly relevant to GMP decision making. This interpretation is immediately meaningful within cleaning-validation practice and remains consistent with the specification-limit-normalization framework previously developed for process capability analysis [ @Yang2026sln]. Consequently, USL-normalization was selected because it provides a common specification scale while preserving both regulatory meaning and natural-cluster membership.

**Generalizability.** \textcolor{blue}{The proposed framework was motivated by two forms of natural clustering: (1) evolutionary processes, including manufacturing and cleaning processes, in which data before and after a process improvement form distinct but related clusters; and (2) cleaning processes in which API-specific cleaning events form natural clusters. Accordingly, this study develops a general multicluster SPC theory and algorithm and demonstrates its application through two pharmaceutical cleaning-validation case studies. The mathematical framework and algorithm are formulated independently of the Equipment A and Equipment B case studies, which are subsequently used to demonstrate implementation of the general methodology. In particular, Equipment B has a dual role: it represents a cleaning-validation process while also representing an evolutionary process because the use of two different cleaning agents creates distinct but related clusters. Thus, the case studies illustrate both API-related clustering within cleaning validation and process-evolution clustering within the same general multicluster framework. The mathematical framework and algorithm are not specific to the particular equipment, APIs, cleaning agents, sampling locations, or analytical methods represented by Equipment A and Equipment B. Provided that appropriate measurements, specification limits, and natural cluster structures can be defined, the same algorithmic framework can be applied to other cleaning-validation processes involving measurements such as DAR, CAR, Mic, or other relevant attributes.}

\textcolor{blue}{The two case studies nevertheless represent only specific realizations of the broader range of conditions that may occur in practice and therefore should not be interpreted as empirical validation of every possible application. Different equipment configurations, API characteristics, cleaning procedures, sampling designs, analytical methods, reporting limits, and data-accumulation patterns may affect the resulting cluster structures, within- and between-cluster variability, and control-chart performance. Before implementation in a substantially different application, practitioners should therefore verify the appropriateness of the selected clustering structure, specification limits, sampling and analytical procedures, Stage 3A reference data, and resulting control-chart performance using data representative of the intended process. The same analytical framework has also been applied to cleaning validation of solid-dosage manufacturing equipment at two Apotex sites, although the present study reports only the Equipment A and Equipment B case studies.}

\textcolor{blue}{More generally, the proposed multicluster SPC framework is not restricted to cleaning-validation processes. It can also be applied to evolutionary manufacturing processes in which data before and after a process change or improvement naturally form distinct but related clusters. For example, observations from a manufacturing process before an improvement can form one cluster, while observations from the improved process can form another cluster. For characteristics with a USL, USL-normalized data can be used to evaluate stability relative to the upper specification boundary and upper capability through $P_{pu}$ as described in } [@Yang2026sln]. \textcolor{blue}{Similarly, for characteristics with an LSL, LSL-normalized data can be used to evaluate stability relative to the lower specification boundary and lower capability through $P_{pl}$} [@Yang2026sln]. \textcolor{blue}{For a characteristic bounded by both USL and LSL, the two perspectives can be combined for stability assessment, while overall capability can be summarized by $P_{pk}=\min(P_{pu},P_{pl})$. Thus, the proposed framework extends beyond cleaning validation to the broader monitoring of manufacturing processes characterized by meaningful specification boundaries and natural or evolutionary cluster structures.}



**Limitations and Future Work.** \textcolor{blue}{The median and MAD are robust statistics that may be less responsive to process shifts than the corresponding benchmark statistics. Future research may investigate alternative event-level statistics that maintain robustness while improving sensitivity to process shifts.} The current $d$-selection algorithm focuses primarily on ARL-based performance criteria and does not explicitly consider the separation between the CL and UCL. Consequently, multiple candidate values of $d$ may satisfy the performance requirements while producing substantially different chart geometries. Future work may investigate optimization criteria that jointly consider ARL performance and the practical interpretability of the resulting control limits.

The present study focuses on Shewhart-type monitoring through the d-CCSSBU-L and d-CCSSBU-S charts. Although effective for detecting moderate-to-large process changes, Shewhart charts are generally less sensitive to small sustained shifts. Extensive research has demonstrated the advantages of cumulative-sum (CUSUM) and exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) control charts for early detection of small process changes. Future work will therefore investigate CUSUM- and EWMA-based extensions of the proposed d-CCSSBU framework to improve sensitivity to subtle shifts in cleaning-validation performance while retaining the distribution-free and cluster-calibrated properties of the proposed methodology.

The current framework is restricted to univariate monitoring. However, multivariate control-chart methodologies have been widely developed and applied when multiple quality characteristics must be monitored simultaneously [@Khusna2020MaxMCUSUM; @Liu1995Multivariate; @Zou2012SpatialRankEWMA]. In practical cleaning-validation programs, multiple residue attributes, analytical methods, and sampling locations may exhibit correlation structures that cannot be adequately characterized by independent univariate charts. Future research will therefore explore multivariate d-CCSSBU control charts capable of simultaneously monitoring multiple cleaning-validation quality attributes, while retaining univariate charts as complementary diagnostic tools for root-cause investigation and signal interpretation.


Finally, this work originated from the development of the CV-SARWAS AI Automation System, which integrates data acquisition, statistical analysis, reporting, and decision support into a unified platform. Recent developments in AI and machine-learning-assisted SPC suggest opportunities to extend traditional stability analysis toward intelligent monitoring systems [@Tran2021MLSPC]. Consistent with emerging FDA guidance on AI-enabled software functions [@FDA2025AIDSF], future research will investigate the implementation of stability analysis, process capability analysis, and automated trend detection as AI-assisted agents within the CV-SARWAS framework, thereby supporting more efficient, scalable, and standardized cleaning-validation lifecycle management.


# Conclusion

**One Theory.** This study developed a multicluster SPC theory for process stability analysis. The theory recognizes that conventional SPC operates under a one-cluster assumption and can therefore be viewed as a special case of multicluster SPC. By treating the natural cluster as the fundamental event-generating structure within a population, the framework extends location and scale monitoring from one-cluster populations to populations comprising multiple natural clusters.

**Two Applications.** The first application is evolutionary process stability monitoring. Process improvements, material substitutions, supplier changes, equipment modifications, analytical-method updates, and other planned operational changes may evolve an existing process into a new process over time. Under this framework, the original process forms one natural cluster and the evolved process forms another. Because the evolved process is derived from the original process, the two clusters are often expected to share many underlying process characteristics. Moreover, the evolved process is typically intended to be equivalent to or better than its predecessor; otherwise, there would be little justification for implementing the change. The proposed framework therefore evaluates whether the two clusters can appropriately share a common SPC reference structure, allowing stability assessment of the evolved process without requiring it to independently accumulate a large reference dataset before monitoring can begin. This capability supports continuous lifecycle monitoring across planned process evolution while preserving accumulated process knowledge.

The second application is naturally multiclustered cleaning-validation process stability monitoring. In this setting, API-specific cleaning events form natural clusters with different location and scale characteristics. The proposed methodology provides a knowledge-driven, risk-based framework for ordering and consolidating natural clusters to construct the d-CCSSBU-L and d-CCSSBU-S charts to monitor cleaning-process stability.

Together, the proposed theory and applications establish a practical framework for stability analysis and ongoing monitoring of multicluster processes. More broadly, the framework demonstrates that scientifically meaningful natural clusters need not be treated as isolated monitoring problems and may, when justified, share a common control-chart reference structure. This capability supports both evolutionary process monitoring and naturally multiclustered process environments in which conventional one-cluster SPC assumptions are no longer adequate.

# Revision Response to Reviewers' Comments

Reviewer 1: 

1. Specification and realized performance of the recommended three-sigma Poisson $\mu$ chart. The revised Discussion recommends the conventional three-sigma Poisson $\mu$  chart as the primary benchmark chart on a process-monitoring basis, while retaining the exact Poisson-quantile chart as a reference. However, the control-limit formula is stated only for the exact-quantile chart (in the chart-construction step); the three-sigma chart's control-limit formula is not given anywhere in the manuscript body, and its realized in-control performance is not reported. For the worked Equipment A case ($\lambda = 0.10$), the three-sigma limit (UCL 2.0974, signalling at a count $\ge 2$) corresponds to an in-control ARL of roughly 214, versus the stated design ARL$_0$ of 740 and roughly 6,450 for the exact-quantile chart (UCL 4.0, signalling at a count $\ge 3$). The lower three-sigma limit is described only as providing "greater sensitivity," without noting the accompanying increase in false-alarm rate. Please state the three-sigma chart's control-limit formula and report its realized ARL$_0$ alongside the sensitivity, so that the recommended chart is fully specified and the sensitivity/false-alarm trade-off is explicit.

**Response:** \textcolor{blue}{Thank you for this helpful observation. We agree that the realized in-control performance and the associated sensitivity–false-alarm trade-off should be made explicit when recommending the conventional three-sigma Poisson $u$ chart. Accordingly, we have added the UCL formula for the conventional three-sigma chart on page 18, lines 701–706 (in blue). We have also revised the Discussion (lines 974–983 on page 30 in blue) to report the realized $ARL_0$ values for Equipment A ($ARL_0 \approx 214$ for the conventional three-sigma chart and $ARL_0 \approx 6466$ for the exact Poisson-quantile chart) and to clarify that the increased sensitivity of the conventional chart is accompanied by a higher in-control false-alarm rate. The revised text therefore makes the sensitivity–false-alarm trade-off explicit and clarifies the respective roles of the two charts.}

2. Limitations sentence, undefined "k" and re-introduced comparability claim. The Limitations and Future Work section states that the optimized d-CCSSBU charts "generally satisfied the benchmark sensitivity criteria at the target shifts of k = 0.5 … and $\rho = 1.05$." The symbol k is not defined anywhere in the revised manuscript — the location-shift grid is now expressed in units of $\rho$- so "k = 0.5" has no referent. The sentence also re-introduces a benchmark-comparability claim that was removed elsewhere in the revision: the revised Abstract states that neither the d-CCSSBU charts nor the $\bar X$-$S$ charts uniformly showed ARL₁ superiority, and the Results show the conventional S chart outperforming the d-CCSSBU-S chart at $\rho$ = 1.05 for CAR. Please remove or rewrite this sentence for consistency, and define any symbol that is retained.

**Response:** \textcolor{blue}{Thank you for pointing this out. We have removed the previous sentence containing the undefined symbol $k$ and the general benchmark-comparability statement. The Limitations and Future Work section (line 1228--line 1230 on page 37 in blue) has been revised to reflect the results more precisely. The revised text now recognizes that the median and MAD, while providing robustness, may be less responsive to process shifts than the corresponding benchmark statistics, and identifies the investigation of alternative robust but more sensitive event-level statistics as an area for future research.}

3. Reporting of $s_Z$ and $\sigma_Z$. The shift grid ρ is expressed in units of $\sigma_Z = max(s_Z, 0.05)$, and the algorithm step instructs the user to report the corresponding values of $s_Z$ and $\sigma_Z$ for the DAR, CAR, and microbial datasets. These numeric values are not reported anywhere in the manuscript (Tables 1-6 contain no $s_Z$ and $\sigma_Z$ column), so the $\rho$ grid cannot be translated back to the measurement (\%USL) scale and it cannot be determined whether the 0.05 floor was binding for any dataset. Please report the $s_Z$ and $\sigma_Z$ values actually used — for example, as an added column in the relevant tables.

**Response:** \textcolor{blue}{Thank you for pointing this out. We have revised Tables 1–4 (ref. page 19, 20, 22, and 23) to report the $s_Z$ and $\sigma_Z$ values used for the DAR, CAR, and Mic datasets. These values are presented in a compact $s_Z/\sigma_Z$ column, which allows the $\rho$ shift grid to be related to the measurement (\%USL) scale and makes it clear whether the $0.05$ floor in $\sigma_Z=\max(s_Z,0.05)$ was binding for each dataset. Tables 5 and 6 were not modified to include these values because these tables report goodness-of-fit results used to determine the appropriate analysis algorithm and do not report the ARL-based shift analyses in which $s_Z$ and $\sigma_Z$ are used. The requested $s_Z$ and $\sigma_Z$ values are therefore reported in Tables 1–4, where they are directly relevant to the shift-grid calculations.}

Reviewer 2: 

1. Preservation of Sampling-Location Relationships During Bootstrap Resampling

Section 2.3.3, Step 11, describes generating synthetic cleaning events by sampling observations separately from each sampling-location stratum. While the procedure preserves the sampling-location-specific observations, it does not necessarily preserve the relationships among locations within the same historical cleaning event. From a cleaning-validation perspective, multiple sampling locations may be influenced by common cleaning conditions, including cleaning-agent concentration, temperature, contact time, and cleaning effectiveness. Please clarify the potential impact of this resampling approach on estimated within-event variability and control limits. A comparison with event-level resampling that preserves the original relationships among sampling locations would help demonstrate the robustness of the proposed approach.

**Response:** \textcolor{blue}{Thank you for this important comment. We agree that location-stratified resampling does not explicitly preserve the within-event relationships among sampling locations and that common cleaning conditions may induce dependence among locations within the same cleaning event. We have therefore revised the manuscript to acknowledge this limitation explicitly and conducted additional sensitivity analyses to evaluate its practical impact on the estimated control limits. Please refer line 992--line 1057 of page 31-page 33 in blue.}

\textcolor{blue}{First, using the available Equipment B data, we compared the proposed location-stratified bootstrap with complete-event bootstrap resampling, which preserves the observed sampling-location relationships within each historical cleaning event. The resulting $UCL_L$ and $UCL_S$ values are reported in Table 7. For the location statistic, the location-stratified bootstrap produced $UCL_L$ values that were equal to or lower than those obtained from complete-event resampling for DAR, CAR, and microbial data. Thus, for the primary location chart, the proposed resampling procedure did not inflate the estimated upper control limit in the investigated cleaning-validation data.}

\textcolor{blue}{Second, we conducted an independent-location normal simulation study to examine the comparison under an idealized setting without the complications of ND observations and within-event dependence. As reported in Table 8, the location-stratified bootstrap closely approximated the control limits obtained from direct complete-event simulation and produced slightly lower $UCL_L$ and $UCL_S$ values.}

\textcolor{blue}{Third, to directly address the reviewer's concern regarding within-event dependence, we conducted an additional correlated-location simulation using a random-effects model that induces positive correlation among sampling locations within the same event. The results are reported in Table 9. The location-stratified bootstrap again produced a lower $UCL_L$ than event-level resampling, whereas the $UCL_S$ comparison reversed direction.}

\textcolor{blue}{Taken together, the genuine-data analysis and the independent- and correlated-location simulations consistently show that, for the location statistic, location-stratified resampling yielded control limits that were either comparable to or more conservative than those obtained from event-level resampling. The scale-statistic results were less consistent and depended on the data structure. We have therefore clarified in the revised manuscript that the scale chart is used as a supplementary diagnostic tool, while the location chart serves as the primary monitoring tool. We have also explicitly identified the lack of preservation of within-event location relationships as a limitation of the proposed location-stratified bootstrap.}

2. Justification of the Stage 3A Calibration Sample Size

The revised manuscript provides additional details regarding Stage 3A calibration and the handling of calibration-limited datasets. However, the selection of 10 cleaning events as the provisional minimum remains insufficiently justified. Since the reliability of control-limit estimation depends on the representativeness and variability of the calibration dataset, please clarify the scientific or statistical rationale for this threshold. It would be helpful to discuss whether the stability of the estimated control limits and out-of-control detection performance was evaluated using larger Stage 3A datasets.

**Response:** \textcolor{blue}{Thank you for this important comment. We agree that two related issues should be distinguished when considering the provisional choice of $n_{3A}=10$: the reliability of control-limit estimation and the out-of-control detection performance of the resulting charts. Please line 1058--1086 on page 33 in blue}

\textcolor{blue}{Regarding control-limit reliability, we do not intend to suggest that $n_{3A}=10$ is a statistically optimal or preferred calibration sample size. As clarified in the revised manuscript, $n_{3A}=10$ was selected as a provisional minimum starting requirement that balances the statistical need for calibration data against the limited availability and slow accumulation of cleaning-validation data. Published Phase I control-chart applications cited in Refs. 11–13 commonly use approximately 20–30 observations or subgroups, and we agree that larger Stage 3A samples provide more reliable control-limit estimation. The revised manuscript therefore explicitly recommends increasing $n_{3A}$ toward 20–30 observations per cluster when sufficient data are available, or using a statistically justified sample size based on Type I error, Type II error, and estimation-reliability considerations. Thus, $n_{3A}=10$ should be interpreted as a practical minimum for initiating stability assessment, rather than as the statistically preferred sample size.}

\textcolor{blue}{This practical consideration is particularly relevant to the proposed multicluster framework because the Stage 3A requirement applies to each cluster. For example, with three clusters, requiring 30 Stage 3A observations per cluster could require approximately 90 observations before prospective monitoring begins, which may substantially delay implementation for data-sparse cleaning-validation applications.}

\textcolor{blue}{Regarding out-of-control detection performance, we evaluated the proposed charts constructed using $n_{3A}=10$ through the Stage 3A ARL$_1$ sensitivity analyses shown in Figures 1 and 3. Relative to the conventional $\bar X$- and $S$-chart benchmarks, the proposed charts did not exhibit a general deterioration in shift-detection performance. The relative performance depended on the residue type and magnitude of the process change: under some investigated conditions the proposed charts had lower ARL$1$, whereas under others the conventional benchmark charts performed better. These results therefore indicate that use of the provisional minimum $n{3A}=10$ did not inherently compromise detection capability relative to the conventional SPC benchmarks under the investigated conditions.}

\textcolor{blue}{We have revised the manuscript accordingly to make clear both the reliability limitation associated with a small Stage 3A calibration sample and the empirical ARL$1$ performance obtained with $n{3A}=10$. Larger Stage 3A samples remain preferred whenever additional data are available.}

3. Rationale for the 70\% USL Calibration Threshold

Section 2.3.2, Step 5, continues to apply a threshold of 70\% of the applicable USL for selecting calibration-eligible cleaning events. Although this may serve as a screening criterion for excluding higher-residue events from baseline estimation, the scientific or statistical justification for selecting this particular threshold remains unclear. Cleaning events with residue results between 70\% and 100\% of the USL may still meet the established cleaning acceptance criteria. Excluding these events could influence the representativeness of the calibration dataset and the resulting control limits. Please clarify the rationale for this threshold and discuss whether alternative thresholds would materially affect calibration eligibility, estimated control limits, or out-of-control detection performance. A sensitivity assessment would strengthen the methodological justification.

**Response:** \textcolor{blue}{Thank you for this important comment. We agree that the previous 70\% USL threshold introduced an additional calibration-eligibility criterion for observations that could still satisfy the established cleaning acceptance specification, and that the selection of this additional threshold was not sufficiently justified for Stage 3. We have therefore removed the 70\% criterion (which is used in Stage 1 where people do not have any information of the process) from the proposed algorithm. Please refer line 368--line375 of page10 in blue}

\textcolor{blue}{In the revised Step 5, a cleaning event is calibration-eligible if $\max_{i=1,\ldots,p}Z_{ti}\le100$, so that calibration eligibility is now defined directly by the applicable USL rather than by an additional 70\% screening threshold. Under this definition, observations between 70\% and 100\% of the USL are no longer excluded solely because of their proximity to the specification limit. Conversely, an observation exceeding 100\% of the applicable USL is outside the established specification and therefore represents an OOS result rather than a routine in-specification cleaning event suitable for baseline calibration. The FDA defines OOS results as results falling outside established specifications or acceptance criteria and provides for their investigation.}

\textcolor{blue}{Accordingly, the revised criterion both addresses the representativeness concern raised by the reviewer and provides a clearer practical basis for calibration-event selection: all events satisfying the applicable specification are eligible for consideration, whereas events containing an OOS observation are excluded from baseline calibration. Because the previous 70\% threshold has been removed rather than retained as a methodological parameter, a sensitivity analysis over alternative arbitrary thresholds is no longer required for the proposed algorithm.}

4. Influence of Nondetect Observations on Monitoring Performance

The revised manuscript provides additional discussion of nondetect observations and explains the rationale for adopting a distribution-free bootstrap approach. However, the potential influence of substantial nondetect proportions on event-level median and MAD statistics, estimated control limits, and detection sensitivity remains insufficiently demonstrated. In particular, repeated substitution at the LOD or LOQ may produce zero-MAD events and reduce sensitivity to residue changes affecting only a subset of sampling locations. Please further clarify these limitations and, where feasible, provide a sensitivity assessment considering different proportions of nondetect observations and analytical reporting limits. Such an assessment would help establish the reliability of the proposed framework when applied to cleaning processes that routinely generate predominantly nondetect results.

**Response:** \textcolor{blue}{Thank you for this important comment. We agree that substantial proportions of ND observations and repeated replacement by a common LOD or LOQ can affect event-level statistics, estimated control limits, and detection sensitivity. We have therefore substantially expanded the Discussion (lines 1096--1138, pages 33--34 in blue) and added Table 10 to quantify the prevalence of ND events in the datasets used in this study.}

\textcolor{blue}{First, regarding the influence on the median, MAD, and estimated control limits, Refs. 46 and 47 and the references therein discuss the effects of replacing ND observations by a constant under assumed distributions. As now stated in the revised manuscript, common upper-bound replacement may increase estimated location statistics while reducing estimated variability when many observations are assigned the same replacement value. Consequently, repeated LOD/LOQ replacement can generate ties and small or zero MAD values and can affect the resulting event-level location and scale statistics and control limits relative to those that would be obtained if the true unobserved values were known. In the proposed implementation, zero or very small MAD values do not prevent chart construction because they are accommodated by the predefined scale floor, $\sigma_t=\max(s_t,0.05)$.}

\textcolor{blue}{Second, to provide an empirical assessment under different observed levels of ND prevalence, we added Table 10. The DAR and CAR datasets span markedly different ND-event proportions: 10.00\% for Equipment A DAR, 100.00\% for Equipment A CAR, 74.00\% for Equipment B DAR, and 84.62\% for Equipment B CAR. Thus, the empirical applications include conditions ranging from relatively low ND prevalence to datasets dominated, or entirely represented, by ND events.}

\textcolor{blue}{Third, we related these observed ND proportions to the ARL$_1$ sensitivity results in Figures 1--4. For Equipment A DAR, with 10.00\% ND events, the d-CCSSBU-L chart showed lower ARL$_1$ than the conventional $\bar X$-chart benchmark over the evaluated shifts, while the d-CCSSBU-S chart did not show a uniform sensitivity disadvantage relative to the conventional $S$ chart. For Equipment A CAR, with 100.00\% ND events, the d-CCSSBU-L chart did not show a general sensitivity disadvantage relative to the $\bar X$ chart, whereas the d-CCSSBU-S chart showed poorer ARL$_1$ performance than the conventional $S$ chart. For Equipment B DAR and CAR, with 74.00\% and 84.62\% ND events, respectively, neither the proposed charts nor the corresponding conventional benchmarks uniformly dominated across the evaluated shifts. Collectively, these results show that substantial ND prevalence does not automatically result in systematically inferior detection performance of the proposed charts relative to the conventional benchmarks, although the results also indicate that sensitivity can be affected, particularly for the scale statistic.}

\textcolor{blue}{We agree that the present empirical results do not constitute a controlled sensitivity experiment in which the ND proportion and LOD/LOQ are independently varied while the underlying data-generating distribution is held fixed. Such an experiment would require assumptions regarding the unobserved distribution below the analytical reporting limit and the censoring mechanism. Because the true values below the LOD/LOQ and the underlying distribution of the CV data are unknown, we have not introduced such assumptions solely for this purpose. Instead, the revised manuscript reports the actual range of ND prevalence represented in the available data and evaluates chart sensitivity under those observed conditions. We have also clarified that LOD/LOQ replacement is an upstream data-handling choice rather than an inherent component of the d-CCSSBU methodology. Step 1 (lines 355--359 on page 9 in blue) explicitly permits another scientifically justified ND-handling procedure, with the resulting data subsequently supplied to the same control-chart algorithm. Different ND proportions, analytical reporting limits, and alternative ND-handling procedures are identified as areas for further investigation.}

5. Stage 3B Monitoring and Generalizability

The revised manuscript provides clearer definitions of Stage 3A, Stage 3B, and retrospective monitoring. The discussion of evolutionary process monitoring is also a useful addition. However, the distinction between retrospective evaluation and prospective Stage 3B monitoring remains unclear in the presented equipment case studies. Please clarify whether the monitoring observations were collected and evaluated prospectively after the control limits had been finalized, or whether the analyses were performed using retrospectively partitioned historical datasets. This distinction is particularly relevant where observations beyond the nominal Stage 3A period are used to supplement calibration. Additionally, while the Equipment A and Equipment B case studies demonstrate the potential applicability of the framework, further discussion is needed regarding its applicability to different equipment configurations, API characteristics, cleaning procedures, sampling designs, and analytical methods. The limitations of the current evidence and the conditions requiring additional verification before implementation should be clearly acknowledged.

**Response:** \textcolor{blue}{Thank you for this important comment. We have revised the manuscript to clarify both the monitoring status of the Equipment A and Equipment B case studies and the limitations of the current evidence regarding generalizability. Please ref line 337-349 on page 9, line1139--1172 on page 35, and line1191--1227 on page 36 in blue. }

\textcolor{blue}{Regarding the distinction between retrospective evaluation and prospective Stage 3B monitoring, the Equipment A case study is a retrospective analysis because all available events are used for stability assessment and no subsequent Stage 3B observations are available. In contrast, the Equipment B data were retrospectively available when this study was conducted, but their original temporal order was preserved. Earlier events were assigned to Stage 3A calibration, and subsequent events were sequentially evaluated according to the Stage 3B procedure. Therefore, the Equipment B case study should be interpreted as a retrospective emulation of prospective Stage 3A/Stage 3B monitoring using historical, time-ordered data, rather than as a real-time prospective data-collection study.}

\textcolor{blue}{We have also clarified the mixed Stage 3A/3B status that may arise in a multicluster control chart. Because different clusters may satisfy their Stage 3A requirements at different times, some clusters may begin Stage 3B monitoring while the remaining clusters continue to accumulate Stage 3A calibration information. During this intermediate period, subsequent observations from clusters that have completed Stage 3A are evaluated against the currently available UCL but are not used to estimate or update that UCL. Only new observations from clusters that remain in Stage 3A contribute additional calibration information. Consequently, the reference UCL for the overall multicluster chart remains provisional until all selected clusters have satisfied their Stage 3A requirements. At that point, the UCL is finalized and the overall chart enters full Stage 3B prospective monitoring. This clarification explains when observations beyond the nominal Stage 3A period may supplement calibration and prevents Stage 3B monitoring observations from being reused for control-limit estimation.}

\textcolor{blue}{Regarding generalizability, the mathematical framework and algorithm are formulated independently of the Equipment A and Equipment B case studies, which are subsequently used to demonstrate implementation of the general methodology. The algorithm therefore does not depend on the particular equipment configurations, APIs, cleaning agents, sampling locations, or analytical methods represented in these two applications. Provided that appropriate measurements, specification limits, and natural cluster structures can be defined, the same framework can be applied to other cleaning-validation and evolutionary manufacturing processes.}

\textcolor{blue}{Nevertheless, we now explicitly acknowledge that the two case studies represent only specific realizations of the broader range of conditions encountered in practice and should not be interpreted as empirical validation of every possible application. Different equipment configurations, API characteristics, cleaning procedures, sampling designs, analytical methods, reporting limits, and data-accumulation patterns may affect the cluster structure, within- and between-cluster variability, control-limit estimation, and monitoring performance. Before implementation in a substantially different application, practitioners should verify the appropriateness of the cluster definition, specification limits, sampling and analytical procedures, representativeness of the Stage 3A reference data, and resulting control-limit and detection performance using data representative of the intended process. The revised Generalizability section now states these limitations and implementation conditions explicitly.}
